title: Ectopic adrenal myelolipoma at the hepatic-adrenal interface mimicking hepatic angiomyolipoma: A case report
abstractText: BACKGROUND Myelolipoma is an extremely rare benign tumor composed of mature adipose tissue and hematopoietic elements. Its non-specific clinical presentation and imaging characteristics make preoperative diagnosis difficult, and it may be misdiagnosed as other fat-containing hepatic tumors, particularly hepatic angiomyolipoma. The tissue origin and pathogenesis of hepatic myelolipoma remain unclear. This report presents a rare case of an ectopic adrenal myelolipoma located at the hepatic-adrenal interface with liver involvement. CASE SUMMARY A 61-year-old woman presented with intermittent right upper abdominal pain for more than 2 months. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a 6.2 cm × 4.2 cm fat-containing mass in the right posterior liver adjacent to the right adrenal gland. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated marked signal loss on opposed-phase images, mild delayed enhancement, and hypointensity in the hepatobiliary phase. Hepatic angiomyolipoma was suspected preoperatively. Given the patient’s symptoms and the lesion’s size (> 6 cm), laparoscopic local resection of the right posterior liver was performed. Histopathological examination showed mature adipose and hematopoietic tissues within the capsule, focal adrenal tissue immediately inside the capsule, and hepatic tissue outside the capsule. These findings supported a diagnosis of ectopic adrenal myelolipoma with liver involvement. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 7. During 19 months of follow-up, her abdominal pain improved, with no documented recurrence or postoperative complications. CONCLUSION Ectopic adrenal myelolipoma should be considered in the differential diagnosis of fat-containing lesions at the hepatic-adrenal interface.

title: Specific molecular signature redefines the role of posterior and para-aortic (D2 plus) lymphadenectomy in gastric cancer: Rethinking surgical indications
abstractText: Posterior and para-aortic (D2 plus) lymphadenectomy is still controversial in gastric cancer surgery, as potential oncologic benefit must be balanced against increased technical complexity. Extended lymph node dissection aims to remove residual regional disease, improve staging, and control locoregional recurrence. This review synthesizes the recent literature on D2 plus in advanced gastric cancer, with particular attention to molecular profiling, response to neoadjuvant therapy, and the role of conversion surgery in oligometastatic disease. D2 plus should not be considered routine but may be evaluated in selected patients with bulky nodes in extragastric regions or isolated para-aortic involvement responding to systemic therapy. Pathological response appears to be the strongest prognostic determinant, and persistent nodal burden after neoadjuvant chemotherapy identifies patients with poor survival. Furthermore, molecular subtypes influence biology and expected benefit from therapy: Microsatellite instable tumors may preserve limited propensity for extensive nodal spread, programmed cell death ligand 1 + expression is associated with sensitivity to immunotherapy, microsatellite stability/epithelial-mesenchymal transition is associated with aggressive behaviour and peritoneal dissemination and may benefit from prophylactic intraperitoneal chemotherapy, while human epidermal growth factor receptor 2+ tumors maintain a more uncertain behaviour. In selected patients with oligometastatic disease, D2 plus may be integrated into a conversion surgery strategy. D2 plus should be adapted to treatment response and biological profiling. Given that residual nodal burden may outweigh primary tumor response, a better understanding of the molecular features of gastric cancer may help identify patients who are most likely to benefit from posterior and para-aortic lymphadenectomy.

title: Traditional Chinese medicine-based nonpharmacological interventions for gastrointestinal recovery after colorectal cancer surgery: A network meta-analysis
abstractText: BACKGROUND Postoperative gastrointestinal dysfunction is a common complication after colorectal cancer (CRC) surgery that delays recovery and prolongs hospitalization. Although traditional Chinese medicine (TCM)-based nonpharmacological interventions have been increasingly used to facilitate postoperative gastrointestinal recovery, their comparative effectiveness remains uncertain. AIM To compare TCM-based nonpharmacological interventions for gastrointestinal recovery after CRC surgery. METHODS Eight databases were searched from inception to April 2025 for randomized controlled trials. Risk of bias was assessed using the RoB 2.0 tool, and the certainty of evidence was evaluated using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation. A frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis was conducted using Stata 18.0 and R software. RESULTS A total of 34 randomized controlled trials involving 3391 participants and 16 interventions were enrolled. Compared with usual care, moxibustion combined with herbal hot compress was associated with shorter time to first postoperative flatus [mean difference (MD): -20.64 hours; 95% confidence interval (CI): -33.43 to -7.85] and time to first bowel sounds (MD = -15.72 hours; 95%CI: -24.72 to -6.72). Acupressure combined with moxibustion was associated with a shorter time to first postoperative defecation (MD = -27.25 hours; 95%CI: -45.88 to -8.62), whereas electroacupuncture was associated with a shorter time to first oral feeding (MD = -22.58 hours; 95%CI: -22.71 to -22.45). Auricular acupressure combined with acupressure was associated with a lower incidence of postoperative complications (odds ratio: 0.30; 95%CI: 0.10-0.89). CONCLUSION TCM-based nonpharmacological interventions may improve gastrointestinal recovery after CRC surgery, but low or very low certainty evidence limits confidence in their comparative effectiveness. The findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

title: Machine learning and logistic regression for ascertainable three-year recurrence status after soft tissue sarcoma surgery
abstractText: BACKGROUND Postoperative local-recurrence estimates could inform surveillance discussions after soft tissue sarcoma surgery, but machine-learning performance can be overstated when model selection is not separated from evaluation or when simpler regression models are not compared. AIM To develop and evaluate a model for binary 3-year local-recurrence status among patients with ascertainable status and compare it with prespecified logistic-regression models. METHODS This retrospective two-institution study analyzed 1035 development patients with ascertainable binary recurrence status at 3 years (331 recurrences) and 212 patients in a second-institution cohort (67 recurrences). The estimand was recurrence-status probability conditional on 3-year status being ascertainable, not cumulative incidence in all postoperative patients. The locked analytical package did not retain reason-specific exclusion counts or the source screening denominator for the second institution. Twelve predictors, 243 configurations across 14 model families, and three ensemble strategies were evaluated by five-fold outer cross-validation repeated five times with five-fold inner tuning. Mean Brier score was the primary selection criterion. The selected CatBoost model was fitted in the complete development cohort, frozen, and applied without recalibration in a protocol-frozen second-institution re-evaluation. RESULTS CatBoost had a mean internal area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.8126 and Brier score of 0.1584. In the second institution, its AUC was 0.8050 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.7433-0.8668], Brier score 0.1615 (95%CI: 0.1331-0.1912), log loss 0.4884 (95%CI: 0.4146-0.5678), calibration intercept 0.148 (95%CI: -0.222 to 0.490), and calibration slope 0.985 (95%CI: 0.703-1.357). The CatBoost-minus-six-variable-logistic differences were -0.0083 for AUC (95%CI: -0.0480 to 0.0299) and 0.0043 for Brier score (95%CI: -0.0112 to 0.0198). A secondary full 12-variable logistic model also showed no material difference from CatBoost. CONCLUSION In the protocol-frozen second-institution re-evaluation, CatBoost retained discrimination but did not demonstrate incremental performance over logistic comparators. The study was not designed or powered to establish equivalence or non-inferiority. Prospective multicenter evaluation using time-to-event outcomes is required before clinical use.

title: Constraining dust properties along the minor axis of Andromeda
abstractText: Previous studies of dust emission in the Andromeda galaxy (M31) based primarily on Herschel data have reported inconsistent radial trends in the dust emissivity index (β), partly due to limited wavelength coverage and the degeneracy between dust temperature (T_̊m dust) and β. We aim to improve the constraints of β determinations and obtain the spatial surface density and temperature distributions at giant molecular cloud scales in M31 by extending the spectral coverage into the millimeter regime and by quantifying the impact of wavelength coverage on the T_̊m dust–β degeneracy. We present the 1.15 mm continuum emission along the minor axis of M31 with the 30 m telescope of the Institut de radioastronomie millimétrique (IRAM). The map has an angular resolution of 11.6'', corresponding to approximately 40 pc at the distance of M31. We used these data with Herschel and 450 and 850 μm maps from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope to perform pixel-by-pixel single-component modified blackbody fitting. Including the 850 μm and 1.15 mm data helps reduce the T_̊m dust–β degeneracy and yields an average emissivity index of β ≈ 1.8, which is systematically lower than values derived from far-infrared–only analyses. Radial analysis shows higher β values in the 5 kpc ring compared to the 10 kpc ring. The elevated β values in the inner 5 kpc may be linked to changes in dust composition, potentially associated with enhanced starlight heating in this region. Millimeter wavelength coverage is important for improving β constraints in M31. The lower β values inferred from the 250--1150 μm spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting suggest possible variations in dust emissivity and highlight the importance of sampling the long-wavelength SED slope in nearby galaxies.

title: Prospects for detecting hot-Jupiter tidal decay through transit timing with the Earth 2.0 mission
abstractText: The orbital decay of hot Jupiters provides a unique opportunity to probe tidal dissipation in star-planet systems. However, despite extensive observational efforts, only one hot Jupiter, namely, WASP-12b, currently exhibits conclusive observational evidence to support orbital decay. Thus, expanding this sample is crucial for establishing a statistical understanding of tidal interactions in planetary systems. Long-term transit timing variations (TTVs) provide a direct observational probe of orbital decay induced by tidal dissipation between a hot Jupiter and its host star. The Earth 2.0 (ET) mission will revisit the original field, delivering high-precision transit timing measurements and extending the observational baseline to approximately 24 years (2009--2033). In this work, we aim to assess the capability of ET to detect orbital decay in hot Jupiters previously observed by . Kepler Kepler We generated four years of simulated ET light curves based on the expected photometric precision and observing cadence of the mission and analyzed them jointly with archival and TESS observations. Using these combined datasets, we performed long-term TTV analyses and predicted the achievable precision for measuring orbital period variations. Kepler We find that ET can substantially improve the precision of orbital decay measurements in hot Jupiter systems by a factor of 7.2. Assuming the stellar tidal quality factor inferred from previous observations, ET is expected to detect orbital decay in three additional hot Jupiter systems. The expanded sample of hot Jupiters with measured orbital decay will establish ET as a powerful probe of tidal dissipation in star–planet systems, offering tighter constraints on stellar tidal quality factors and new insights into the tidal evolution of hot Jupiters.

title: Impact of the large-scale environment on the baryonic scaling relations of disc galaxies: Insights from the GASP survey
abstractText: The Tully--Fisher relation (TFR) and the specific angular momentum--mass relation (SAMR) link the baryonic content of a disc to its kinematics and dynamics. Hence, these scaling relations should bear the imprints of any process removing baryons or altering their kinematics, such as those acting in clusters of galaxies. We tested this scenario using the MUSE survey `GAs Stripping Phenomena in galaxies' (GASP), which targets field, group, and cluster members at z ≈ 0.05 and various stages of ram pressure stripping. For the 81 discs with favourable inclinations, we measured the distribution and kinematics of stars and ionised gas and their specific angular momenta. Within their scatter, the stellar and baryonic relations show no significant dependence on the large-scale environment. The TFRs have slopes of α ≈ 3.6 and ≈ 3.5 for any kinematic tracer, and the SAMRs have α ≈ 0.65--0.75, as predicted by tidal torque theory. The same holds for the ten S0-S0/as in our sample, consistent with the `faded spiral' formation scenario. Only the gas SAMR shows an environmental signature, with ram pressure stripped galaxies lying ≈ 0.16 dex below unperturbed ones. This offset is mostly due to their enhanced star formation rate and thus higher gas mass when inferred through the Schmidt-Kennicutt law rather than to kinematic perturbations or disc truncation. Our results suggest that within the area probed by MUSE (łesssim6 disc scale lengths), these discs have preserved the angular momentum acquired at formation not only from cluster processes and pre-processing in filaments but also from mergers and ejective feedback acting in any environment.

title: The impact of MUSE sky subtraction on unresolved stellar population end products. Study cases of NGC,1097 and NGC,1433
abstractText: One of the main steps in data reduction for ground-based astronomy is sky subtraction. For extended objects, it is necessary to observe dedicated sky frames, usually with air-mass values similar to the target's, using different pointing strategies. However, it is not well documented how different observing strategies can affect the science end product. In particular, with the use of the Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE/VLT), the sky subtraction step can yield distinct stellar population products, such as age, metallicity, and α enhancement. To address this , we considered two case studies , NGC,1097 and NGC,1433, seeking to investigate: ( ) the sky stability in observations taken consecutively i over a period of two hours with thin sky transparency and air-mass values of 1.25-1.05, and ( ) the impact of different sky conditions on the same target. Among our main results, we find that for galaxies with 0.0014 łeq z łeq 0.0077, the sky line ii NI łambda5200 coincides with the Mg_b bandpass, which is essential for metallicity measurements, and highlights the need for proper sky subtraction. In addition, for regions with relative fluxes above 10 with respect to the sky in NGC,1097, sky frames with variation up to sim18% still retrieve consistent stellar population properties -- in this case, this corresponds to flux values of ≥ 1500 , 10^ -20 erg , -1 , cm^ -2 , and Johnson-V sim19.0. In contrast, when comparing data from different nights for NGC,1433, fainter regions suffer greatly from distinct sky conditions, especially in metallicity measurements, which range from ∼-0.2 to ∼+0.2; this strongly affects the interpretation of the stellar mass assembly . This study is the first of its kind and highlights the importance of proper sky subtraction, providing insights regarding data limitations and black and the origin of the gas (i.e. mergers might bring metal-poor gas while an in-situ burst of star formation can yield metal-rich stars) observational strategies for future observations with MUSE.

title: Mitigating variance shrinkage in multitask galaxy property inference from imaging data via statistical manifold alignment
abstractText: Inferring photometric redshifts (z) and key stellar population properties (łog(M_*/ _⊙), D_n 4000, and mathrm M H δ_A) directly from multiband imaging is increasingly critical for spectroscopically limited large surveys such as LSST and CSST. However, conventional pointwise loss functions (e.g., mean squared error or Huber loss) employed in deep neural networks often induce ``variance shrinkage''---a regression-to-the-mean effect that contracts predicted variances, distorts nonlinear physical manifolds (such as bimodal distributions), and truncates heavy-tailed populations. Here, we present ViTMultiTask, a vision transformer framework that incorporates a multiscale maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss to enforce higher-order joint distribution alignment in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Trained on 83,846 galaxies from Subaru HSC five-band (g,r,i,z,y) imaging cross-matched with DESI Data Release 1 Bright Galaxy Survey spectra, the model achieves high point-estimate precision on an independent test set of 5,000 galaxies: σ_ NMAD = 0.020 for z, 0.169, for łog(M_*/ _⊙), 0.073 for D_n 4000, and 1.185, δ_A. Ablation experiments demonstrate that incorporating the MMD loss effectively mitigates variance shrinkage and more accurately reproduces the observed spectroscopic parameter distributions (including bimodal structures and heavy tails), while maintaining point-estimate accuracy statistically consistent with the baseline (with RMSE changes łe 3.5%) and catastrophic outlier rates fully comparable to the baseline. This kernel-based manifold alignment offers a statistically grounded and practical paradigm for comprehensive galaxy property inference in the deep imaging era. M for mathrm H

title: Numerical experiments on sunspot penumbral flows
abstractText: We present 3D radiative magnetohydrodynamic simulations of sunspots with a self-consistently generated penumbra. We analyze the impact of resolution, surrounding opposite-polarity fields, and subsurface large-scale flows on the structure and stability of the simulated penumbra. Extended penumbral filaments were obtained for a subset of the simulations. These were run with a resolution of 25 km (15 km) in the horizontal (vertical) direction, and with initial conditions favoring fields with strong horizontal components in the penumbral region. The surface velocities in these simulations are consistent with observations of Evershed flow. The main driving mechanism remains the same as illustrated in previous simulations. The most successful simulations produce extended penumbrae using a potential magnetic field top boundary, in contrast to previous simulations of extended penumbra with an artificial enhancement of the horizontal magnetic field at the top boundary.

title: Inferring accretion bursts in intermediate-mass protostars from asteroseismic imprints
abstractText: During star formation, objects may gain the majority of their final mass through regular and intense bursts of mass accretion. For burst events of the FU Orionis-type (FUor), accretion rates can climb as high as 10^ -3 in short windows of time, amounting to just a few percent of the main accretion phase. Some bursters had not been observed in the preceding quiescent stage, making their classification as FUors difficult. To study the occurrence of such events observationally, signatures of the current accretion bursts and tracers of recent bursts are crucial. In this work, we investigate the potential to identify current accretion bursts and detect recent bursts in protostars and pre-main sequence (pre-MS) stars of intermediate mass using asteroseismology. The aim is to characterize theoretical period-spacing diagrams of pre-MS gravity-mode (g-mode) pulsators that have undergone accretion bursts. We used the stellar structure and evolution code to evolve stellar models from the protostellar seed phase of 0.01 MESA and 1.5 ̊sun up to 4.0 with a constant accretion rate of 10^ -6 A single accretion burst was initialized during the accretion phase. The stellar oscillation code GYRE was employed to compute the resulting asteroseismic properties of the models. Accretion bursts of up to 10^ -3 are sufficient to cause the convective cores of the models to recede, leaving behind a chemical trace that is manifested in the form of quasi-periodic dips in the g-mode period spacing. This effect is strongest during the outburst, but also lingers for up to 475 years before the convective core is re-established and the dips are gone. Our experiment shows that a single accretion burst leaves an imprint in the deep interiors of protostars and pre-MS stars of intermediate mass and that this imprint can be captured with asteroseismology. Well-resolved g-mode pulsations of young stellar objects may therefore help identify current and recent accretion bursts. Our results are most conclusive for burst magnitudes greater than 1 -4 corresponding to FUor-type bursts.

title: The long-period central star of the planetary nebula MPAJ1508-6455
abstractText: A significant fraction of planetary nebulae have been shown to host short-period binary central stars, but longer-period central stars are scarcer. We characterise the central star of the planetary nebula MPAJ1508-6455, which has previously been claimed to be an intermediate-period binary with a period of approximately 12 days. We studied archival and catalogue photometry to probe the previously reported photometric variability and binary spectral energy distribution. We used long-term high-resolution spectroscopic monitoring to measure the radial velocity curves of the two components of the central binary, and to derive their atmospheric parameters. We also undertook kinematical and chemical abundance analyses of the nebula itself. The orbital period of the central binary of exceeds five years and is highly eccentric. The binary comprises a relatively low-temperature sdO-type central star and a spun-up K-type giant companion. The Kiel mass of the central star is approximately half the dynamical mass derived from the radial velocities. While the systemic velocity and inclination of the nebula are consistent with the radial velocities of the binary, its abundance pattern adds support for a lower-mass progenitor that did not experience hot bottom burning (and is thus more consistent with the Kiel mass than the mass derived from the radial velocities). To the best of our knowledge, the central star of is only the fourth planetary nebula central star to have a spectroscopically confirmed orbital period longer than one year.

title: A biogeographic shift toward tropical and subtropical freshwater invaders in Massachusetts, USA (1831–2020)
abstractText: Climate change is reshaping species distributions worldwide with tropical and subtropical taxa increasingly expanding their ranges poleward. While most studies have modeled potential future shifts under warming scenarios, empirical evidence confirming that this is already underway remains limited, particularly in freshwater ecosystems. Here, we present a comprehensive historical dataset spanning 1831 to 2020 that provides evidence of climate-driven range expansion in the northeastern United States. Rising temperatures have enabled the establishment and survival of warm-adapted invasive species in freshwater systems of Massachusetts that were previously too cold to sustain overwintering populations. While of the twelve aquatic invasive species documented in the state from 1831 to 1990, only two were of tropical or subtropical origin, this ratio increased to four of the seven species established between 1990 and 2010. This shift reflects a major ecological transition mainly driven by climate warming and highlights that climate change is not only altering the potential for future invasions but is actively shaping contemporary dynamics. These findings underscore the urgent need to incorporate climate trajectories into invasive species risk assessments and management strategies for temperate freshwater ecosystems.

title: Epibiont responses to a native and non-native foundation species across a gradient of intertidal stress
abstractText: Non-native foundation species can be detrimental when they displace native species or facilitate non-native species, but they may benefit native species by providing habitat or moderating stressful environments. Interspecific competition and epibiont responses were tested in experimental treatments of two seagrass foundation species (non-native Nanozostera japonica , native Zostera marina , and mixture) along an intertidal stress gradient. Based on this additive design, Z. marina , which has a larger shoot size, was the competitive dominant but performed poorly at higher intertidal elevation, where N. japonica has created novel seagrass habitat. Species using these seagrasses as habitat, including epiphytes and epifauna, responded more to physiological stress than to foundation species identity. Across two sites and three intertidal zones, variation of epiphyte and epifauna load always occurred: generally, epiphyte and epifaunal load increased at lower zones. While the epifauna community mostly did not differ between the two species, N. japonica occasionally had a higher epiphyte and epifauna load. This foundation species difference was moderated in mixture, because of instances of reduced epiphytes or epifauna on N. japonica when Z. marina co-occurred; however, growing in mixture did not affect use of Z. marina habitat. Non-native epifauna made up 30% of invertebrates on seagrass and were not more common on the non-native foundation species or at the higher vegetated zone it has generated. The non-native and native foundation species provided mostly functionally-redundant habitat, which may arise from epibionts using seagrass as structure, not for food resources.

title: Perlindungan Hukum Terhadap Benda Sitaan Milik Pihak Ketiga Sebagai Barang Bukti Dalam Proses Peradilan Pidana
abstractText: Pasal 44 Undang-Undang Nomor 8 Tahun 1981 tentang Hukum Acara Pidana (KUHAP) mewajibkan penyimpanan benda sitaan di Rumah Penyimpanan Benda Sitaan Negara (Rupbasan) guna menjamin keutuhan, keamanan, dan nilai barang bukti sepanjang proses peradilan berlangsung. Namun, praktik di Rupbasan Kelas I Padang masih terdapat benda sitaan yang mengalami kerusakan, hilang, atau menurun nilainya. Penelitian ini mengkaji tentang penyitaan terhadap barang sitaan milik pihak ketiga sebagai barang bukti dalam proses peradilan pidana oleh Rumah Penyimpanan Benda Sitaan Negara Kelas I Padang serta perlindungan hukum oleh Rumah Penyimpanan Benda Sitaan Negara kelas I Padang terhadap benda sitaan negara sebagai barang bukti dalam proses peradilan pidana. Pendekatan penelitian ini adalah yuridis empiris didukung pendekatan yuridis normatif. Dari hasil penelitian diperoleh hasil bahwa penyitaan barang sitaan milik pihak ketiga sebagai barang bukti dalam proses peradilan pidana dimulai dari adanya dugaan tindak pidana dan identifikasi relevansi benda dengan perkara. Penempatan benda sitaan dilakukan menurut sifat dan tingkat risikonya. dilakukan pengawasan agar tidak terjadi penyalahgunaan. Perlindungan Hukum terhadap benda sitaan negara dilakukan dalam bentuk: 1) Perlindungan fisik melalui penyimpanan yang sesuai dengan sifat benda sitaan, pembatasan akses petugas, kontrol administratif, dan larangan penggunaan di luar kebutuhan peradilan. 2) Perlindungan terhadap nilai ekonomis, dilakukan dalam bentuk menjaga keaslian dan validitas barang bukti melalui kesinambungan penguasaan atau chain of custody. 3) Perlindungan hukum pada saat penentuan status akhir benda sitaan melalui putusan pengadilan yaitu pengembalian kepada yang berhak atas benda tersebut.

title: Still room for more: ascidian community composition changes in Southern California over 30 years
abstractText: The productivity and diversity of marine ecosystems are often threatened by the presence of invasive species. The Southern California Bight contains two of the busiest international shipping ports in the United States and is therefore susceptible to ecological changes due to invasive species. Fouling communities in harbors and marinas can be early recipients of non-native species, and are therefore excellent monitoring locations. The goal of this study is to track the arrival and persistence of non-native ascidian species in Southern California fouling communities, and to document changes in community structure over the past 30 years. Changes in ascidian community composition on artificial structures were determined by redoing surveys in 2024 that were previously done in 2019–2020 and 1994–2000. The community composition between 1994–2000 and 2024, and 2019–2020 and 2024 was compared using nMDS plots and associated ANOSIM and SIMPER statistics. The species ranges between 1994–2000 and 2024 were also compared. The community composition changed substantially between the 1994–2000 and 2024 surveys, but not between 2019–2020 and 2024. Five new species were identified in the 2024 survey ( Aplidium sp., Botrylloides perspicuus , Corella japonica , Polyclinum constellatum and Symplegma brakenhielmi ). Ascidiella aspersa has spread along the entire Southern California coastline since its first record in the 2019–2020 survey. The proportion of non-native species that are increasing in abundance has been declining recently in Southern California, suggesting that non-native species could be experiencing more competition from newly established non-native species such as Ascidiella aspersa that are expanding their ranges. In marine communities where non-native species are likely to continue establishing and/or expanding their ranges, long term studies can identify changes in community composition over time.

title: The nonnative species biomass problem: despite lower numbers, the biomass of nonnative fish and snails equals that of native species in a Florida spring
abstractText: Invasions by nonnative species pose a major threat to freshwater ecosystem function and integrity. Freshwater springs, particularly those in Florida, are threatened by loss of water quantity, degradation of water quality, and invasions of nonnative species, the last of which exacerbate the other problems. Most studies quantify the abundance of nonnative species by numbers of individuals, but the average size of species also is important as large species may have greater impacts on systems than small species. Therefore, we evaluated the biomass of native and nonnative fish and snails in a first magnitude spring in Florida. We used seine, snorkel, and video surveys to sample fish and random substrate quadrat samples to sample snails. We measured individuals of all species and calculated biomasses from weights estimated from length measurements. For both fish and snails, the native species outnumbered the nonnative species. Small poeciliids and killifish were the most numerous fish, whereas tiny hydrobiid snails were the most numerous snails. In contrast, most of the nonnative fish and snails were as large or larger than the largest native fish and snails, producing aggregate biomasses of nonnative species that were roughly equivalent to those for fish and snails. Given the greater impact of large-bodied organisms on ecosystem processes, these nonnative species likely have a much greater impact on this spring than their numbers would suggest.

title: Will the real Melanoides tuberculata please stand up? Taxonomically troubling thiarids (Gastropoda, Thiaridae) and multitudes of misidentified Melanoides spp. introduced to Hawai‘i
abstractText: Thiaridae are aquatic gastropods inhabiting fresh and brackish waters across tropical to warm temperate regions worldwide. Their largely parthenogenetic reproduction, brood care, broad ecological tolerances, and rapid growth have made several species highly effective colonizers and globally invasive pests, often displacing native species and acting as disease vectors. Despite this, thiarid diversity has rarely been evaluated using modern integrative approaches, and their taxonomy remains confused. In Hawai‘i, six species of thiarids have been reported, but their identities and validity have been uncertain. Here, we reassess the diversity, identity, and status of thiarids in Hawai‘i using an integrative taxonomic framework combining mitochondrial (COI, 16S) and nuclear (28S) sequence data, shell morphology, and comparisons with available type material. Phylogenetic analyses recovered seven distinct thiarid lineages in Hawai‘i that we recognize as species, with an additional species identified from shell material alone. All are introduced to the islands. Specimens historically identified as Melanoides tuberculata were found to be polyphyletic, and we restrict the application of that name to a lineage consistent with type material and detected only in pet stores on O‘ahu. Moreover, we demonstrate that the canoe snails brought to Hawai‘i by Polynesians are not Melanoides tuberculata as refined here. To stabilize the taxonomy of two globally invasive pests, we designate lectotypes for Nerita tuberculata O. F. Müller, 1774 and Buccinum scabrum O. F. Müller, 1774. Our results demonstrate that persistent misidentification of invasive thiarids, often mistaken for native or novel taxa, has obscured their origins, diversity, and biogeographic history in Hawai‘i. Accurate taxonomy requires an integrative approach that unites molecular, morphological, and historical data. Failure to do so compromises ecological inference and weakens management and conservation outcomes.

title: Sportfish trajectories during bigheaded carp expansion in the Mississippi River floodplain
abstractText: Bigheaded carps ( Hypophthalmichthys spp.) have expanded throughout a large section of the Mississippi River basin, yet their potential influences on recreational fisheries within floodplain lakes remain poorly understood. Detecting ecological responses to invasive species in large floodplain networks is challenging due to gradual invasion dynamics, spatial variability in invasion intensity, and limited long-term datasets. We used standardized electrofishing records from 11 floodplain lakes monitored between 1987 and 2025 to evaluate long-term sportfish trajectories during carp expansion. Lakes were classified by hydrologic connectivity as batture lakes (hydrologically connected; inside the Mississippi River levees) or non-batture lakes (less connected; outside the levees). Temporal trends in catch per effort were evaluated using visualization approaches, correlation analyses, and mixed-effects models. Sportfish trajectories differed between batture and non-batture lakes, with multiple species exhibiting consistent declining trends in batture lakes. In contrast, trajectories outside the batture were generally more variable and often centered near stable or weakly directional trends. Although annual declines of 2–4% were modest, they translate into substantial cumulative reductions over multidecadal timescales. Because these data reflect long-term monitoring, observed patterns represent broad ecological trajectories during bigheaded carp expansion rather than direct evidence of causation.

title: The response of smallmouth bass populations in inland lakes to recent invasion by round goby
abstractText: The round goby, Neogobius melanostomus , a Ponto-Caspian invader of the Laurentian Great Lakes, is now one of the dominant nearshore prey species. Nearshore predators, such as smallmouth bass ( Micropterus dolomieu ), are benefitting from high round goby abundance and now attain larger body sizes and are generally in better condition. Round goby are beginning to spread to smaller inland lakes in North America, yet the potential impacts to native fishes in these systems are relatively unknown and difficult to predict based on studies from the Great Lakes. Here, we investigated the impact of the round goby on smallmouth bass condition (weight-at-length) and growth (length-at-age) in three invaded inland lakes using body size and age measurements collected by a standardized monitoring program, which we compared to a suite of similar, uninvaded lakes. The condition of smallmouth bass populations in the invaded lakes remained stable in the ~10 years following goby invasion. However, bass in invaded lakes generally exhibited larger asymptotic lengths ( L ∞ ) coupled with slower rates of approaching those lengths ( k ), although responses varied among populations and sampling periods. Reference populations showed the opposite pattern, suggesting the potential for larger maximum body size where round goby are available. Our study shows the potential for inter-lake variability in the response of a top predator to recent invasion of a novel prey, and also highlights that the general benefits to smallmouth bass populations following invasion by round goby seen in the Great Lakes may not be a universal consequence in smaller inland lakes.

title: Authority, trust, and access: re-examining students' choices in the digital information landscape
abstractText: Purpose This study examines how students engage with academic library digital collections by applying the Theory of Planned Behavior and digital divide framework. It aims to identify how attitudes, social expectations, and two forms of perceived control (information literacy self-efficacy and digital access conditions) influence students' intentions and use of digital resources. By distinguishing between cognitive skills and access-related barriers, the research seeks to clarify what drives or limits effective use of library systems and inform strategies to improve equitable digital engagement in higher education. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a survey-based quantitative design grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior. Students completed a structured questionnaire measuring attitudes, subjective norms, internal and external perceived behavioral control, behavioral intention, and self-reported use of digital collections. Findings Findings show that attitudes and subjective norms strongly predict students' intentions to use digital library collections, and intention is the primary driver of actual use. External perceived behavioral control (digital access conditions) significantly strengthens the link between intention and behavior and mediates the effects of attitudes and norms on intention. In contrast, internal control (information literacy self-efficacy) does not significantly predict, mediate or moderate outcomes, indicating that access-related factors rather than cognitive skills are the key constraint on effective digital library use. Originality/value This study is original in distinguishing internal and external forms of perceived behavioral control within a TPB framework. It shows that only access-related factors function as true behavioral control, offering a novel integration of TPB and digital divide theory in explaining digital library use.

title: From data to resilience: examining how and when AI-powered data systems enhance manufacturers' digital resilience
abstractText: Purpose This study investigates how artificial intelligence (AI)-powered data systems enhance manufacturers' digital resilience through dynamic knowledge management and under which contextual conditions these effects are strengthened or weakened. Design/methodology/approach Two-wave survey data from 331 Chinese manufacturing firms are analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrap procedures. Findings The AI-powered data systems significantly improve digital resilience both directly and indirectly through dynamic knowledge integration and dynamic knowledge reconfiguration. Moreover, AI strategic flexibility and environmental hostility strengthen the effects of the three AI-powered capabilities on dynamic knowledge management, thereby amplifying their indirect impact on digital resilience. Practical implications The findings highlight the need to treat AI-powered data systems as strategic, knowledge-centric infrastructures. Managers should invest in integrated AI architectures, cultivate dynamic knowledge processes, and purposefully build AI strategic flexibility, particularly in hostile environments, to unlock resilience gains. Originality/value By specifying dynamic knowledge integration and dynamic knowledge reconfiguration as mediating mechanisms and identifying AI strategic flexibility and environmental hostility as critical boundary conditions, it advances AI strategy, knowledge management, and dynamic capability research in emerging-market manufacturing.

title: S³: A Multicriteria Pre-Deployment Scoring Protocol for Enterprise Small Language Model Selection
abstractText: Technology managers lack a systematic protocol for determining which enterprise workloads are safe for local small language model deployment. We introduce S³ (Suitability Score for SLM Selection), a multicriteria framework that scores workloads across six dimensions, Task Complexity, Output Structure, Stakeholder Risk, Data Sensitivity, Latency Tolerance, and Volume Load, and assigns them to Pure SLM, Hybrid, or LLM-Only tiers before inference. Non-compensatory gate rules enforce safety constraints for high-stakes scenarios, ensuring that life-critical or expert-level generative tasks are never assigned to a local model regardless of their aggregate score. Thresholds calibrated on an independent use-case set correctly predicted all eight held-out tier assignments across six industries, with Pure SLM tiers achieving at least 95% LLM parity.

title: A framework for outpatient CAR-T monitoring to support Canadian CAR-T capacity building
abstractText: Introduction: why outpatient CAR-T therapy now in Canada? Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has significantly improved outcomes, including sustained remissions and even cures, for patients with refractory or relapsed B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), and multiple myeloma (MM).1-8 CAR-T products differ by antigen target, such as CD19 and B cell maturation antigen (BCMA); and by co-stimulatory domain, which is either CD28 (e.g., axicabtagene ciloleucel, brexucabtagene autoleucel) or 4-1BB (e.g., tisagenlecleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, idecabtagene vicleucel). Prior to CAR-T availability, patients with relapsed hematologic malignancies experienced poor outcomes. For example, in patients with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphomas, the median overall survival was 6.2 months. prior to access to CAR-T therapy.9 These outcomes are balanced by CAR-T therapy-associated toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). Despite the substantial clinical benefits observed with CAR T-cell therapy, treatment is associated with distinct immune-mediated toxicities, including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity (ICANs). Although these adverse events are generally manageable with established treatment algorithms and are often reversible, severe toxicities, resulting in organ dysfunction and occasionally death, may occur and can necessitate ICU-level care. Enhanced understanding of toxicity kinetics, earlier intervention strategies, and the availability of effective management approaches such as tocilizumab and corticosteroids have improved the safety profile of CAR T-cell therapy. Early interventions, such as tocilizumab (anti-IL-6R) and corticosteroids, can attenuate the severity of these toxicities. Given the potential for severe toxicities, CAR-T has traditionally been administered and monitored in an inpatient hospital setting.

title: Parents’ perceptions of doll and tablet play
abstractText: Purpose Parents play a central role in shaping children’s play opportunities through their perceptions about the developmental value of different toys. This study aims to examine how parents perceive traditional toys (dolls) relative to digital devices (tablets), whether these perceptions change following children’s randomly assigned play experiences, and whether parental perceptions relate to children’s play engagement at home during the intervention. Design/methodology/approach In a six-to-eight-week home-based intervention, children aged 4–8 years (N = 81) were randomly assigned to receive either dolls or a tablet pre-loaded with open-ended games. Parents reported their perceptions of both toy types before and after the intervention and completed play diaries reporting children’s play frequency with each type of toy. Findings Parents reported positive perceptions of both dolls and tablets pre-and post-intervention. Perceptions of dolls were moderated by child sex, with dolls viewed as more beneficial for girls than for boys. Most perceptions remained stable across time, except for an increased perception that dolls promote body and ethnic diversity among parents in the doll condition. Parents’ pre-intervention perceptions about enjoyment were associated with children’s play frequency over the course of the intervention period. Originality/value The study builds on evidence that parental perceptions of traditional and digital play are shaped by gendered perceptions and shows exposing children to specific kinds of toys at home changes these perceptions.

title: From language to world states: a survey of world models in multimodal reasoning
abstractText: Multimodal reasoning is expanding from interpreting a single observation to understanding dynamic environments and how they evolve. This shift poses new challenges for multimodal systems: they must continuously update their understanding of the environment and anticipate how actions may change it. World models provide a state-centered framework to address this challenge. They organize multimodal observations into task-relevant states. These states can be continuously maintained and updated as the environment evolves, and can support the simulation of future states and action consequences, thereby providing a foundation for downstream reasoning, planning and action. From a functional perspective, this survey reviews the emerging intersection of world models and multimodal reasoning. This survey examines the intersection between world models and multimodal reasoning at two complementary levels: the mechanistic level focuses on how world states support reasoning, while the system level considers how these mechanisms are instantiated as functional roles in multimodal reasoning systems. First, at the mechanistic level, the authors examine the differences and complementarities between language-centered intermediate reasoning traces and state-centered world-model reasoning. The authors further analyze how task-relevant states support multimodal reasoning by enabling persistent state maintenance, evidence-driven updates and simulations conditioned on actions or interventions. Second, at the system level, the authors group existing studies into three overlapping functional roles: temporal and imaginative state reasoning, structured-state reasoning and action-coupled state reasoning. Based on this functional taxonomy, the authors further review advances in world models across various environments and summarize the corresponding evaluation resources. Overall, this survey examines an emerging, more stateful paradigm in multimodal reasoning enabled by world models. This paradigm does not replace language-based or other multimodal forms of reasoning. Instead, it complements them with world-model states that support the persistent maintenance and continual updating of task-relevant information, as well as the simulation of possible futures. By systematically reviewing these developments, this survey seeks to deepen the understanding of the evolving foundations of multimodal reasoning and to provide a useful reference for future research and innovation in this rapidly advancing field.

title: Impact of the use of low-cost technology on the performance of unorganized retailers: a resource dependence view
abstractText: Purpose Grounded in resource dependence theory (RDT), this study empirically examines how low-cost technology adoption, specifically mobile procurement applications, influences the performance of unorganized retailers (URs). The study investigates the mediating role of procurement control capability (PCC), a capability that may reduce environmental dependence by integrating procurement autonomy and uncertainty reduction. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a quantitative research design, collecting cross-sectional data from 301 URs across three major cities in North and Central India. The hypothesized relationships were tested using partial least squares - structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyze the pathways linking technology adoption, PCC and UR performance. Findings Technology adoption does not exert a significant direct effect on performance. Instead, PCC completely mediates the relationship, suggesting that adoption is associated with performance improvements when it strengthens retailers' procurement control. Specifically, mobile procurement apps appear to increase autonomy in product, supplier and offer decisions while reducing uncertainties in stock, price and delivery. Originality/value This study is among the first to integrate autonomy and uncertainty reduction into a unified construct (PCC) and demonstrate its mediating role in the adoption–performance relationship for unorganized retailers. By framing PCC as a dependency-reducing capability, the study extends RDT to resource-constrained digital contexts and contributes to literature on technology-enabled capability transformation in emerging market retail.

title: How do agribusiness start-ups apply the circular economy? Evidence based on the resolve framework
abstractText: Purpose This study aims to investigate how agribusiness start-ups, known as agtechs, adopt circular economy strategies, using the ReSOLVE framework as its theoretical foundation, to understand patterns of circularity implementation within these organisations. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a quantitative approach combining partial least squares structural equation modelling and multidimensional scaling. Data were collected through a questionnaire administered to 155 Brazilian agtechs. Findings The findings reveal a predominance of circular practices focused on the internal efficiency of agtechs, particularly those associated with the actions of optimise, loop and exchange. More collaborative actions, such as regenerate, virtualise and share, were found to be less developed. This pattern suggests a lower level of collaborative maturity, indicating that circularity remains concentrated in internally driven organisational initiatives. Practical implications The findings provide valuable insights for stakeholders, outlining strategies capable of strengthening circularity within the agribusiness sector. Social implications By identifying pathways for implementing circularity within the agribusiness sector, this study contributes to achieving targets related to Sustainable Development Goal 12 of the 2030 Agenda, which promotes responsible consumption and production patterns. Originality/value This study advances the circular economy literature by investigating adoption patterns of the strategies encompassed within the ReSOLVE framework, moving beyond the predominantly descriptive approach to identifying circular practices found in previous studies. Consequently, it extends the application of the ReSOLVE framework as an analytical tool for understanding the circular transition.

title: Parametric design of LPBF Ti-6Al-4V rhombic dodecahedron and Voronoi lattice structures for potential orthopedic applications
abstractText: Purpose This study aims to investigate a unified parametric design framework for laser powder bed fusion (LPBF)-fabricated Ti-6Al-4V scaffolds and compares two architectural classes: a regular rhombic dodecahedron lattice and a stochastic Voronoi-based lattice, with emphasis on macrostructure and mechanical performance. Design/methodology/approach Scaffold geometries were parametrically defined within geometric and manufacturability constraints using open-source mathematical formulations. Specimens were manufactured by LPBF and characterized via gravimetric analysis, X-ray micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) and quasi-static compression testing. Findings Measured structural porosity ranged from ∼59 % to ∼80 %. For rhombic dodecahedron lattices, porosity decreased relative to STL models as unit-cell size decreased, with deviations of 7%–15 %. Voronoi scaffolds showed smaller deviations (−1.5% to 4%). Mechanical properties were strongly correlated with measured porosity. Rhombic dodecahedron structures exhibited Young’s modulus of 1.3–3.7 GPa and apparent yield strength of 41–154 MPa, exceeding those of Voronoi structures (0.9–2.6 GPa and 19–99 MPa, respectively). At fixed geometric parameters, mechanical properties varied approximately linearly with porosity. The governing structural factors differed by topology, with strut number dominating in regular lattices and strut thickness and organic factor governing in stochastic lattices. The results are limited to the investigated geometries and LPBF processing conditions. Fatigue, permeability, biological response and full-scale implant validation were outside the scope of this study. Originality/value The proposed framework enables a direct comparison of regular and stochastic Ti-6Al-4V scaffold architectures fabricated by LPBF and explicitly quantifies discrepancies between nominal CAD designs and as-built structures. By linking topology to manufacturability, porosity deviation and mechanical performance, the study identifies topology-dependent governing parameters: unit-cell size and strut thickness for regular lattices and strut thickness combined with organic factor for stochastic lattices. These results provide design guidelines that incorporate fabrication realities into the optimization of load-bearing orthopedic implants.

title: Burnout and stigma as barriers to mental healthcare in medical students
abstractText: Purpose This study aims to assess burnout among medical students in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and to determine barriers that prevent them from accessing available mental health services and the impact of stigma. Design/methodology/approach This cross-sectional study was conducted in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia from August to December 2023. The inclusion criteria were medical students of both genders enrolled from the first to the sixth academic years at governmental universities in Jeddah. The exclusion criteria were students in other colleges, students from private universities and those residing outside Jeddah. A purposive online sample of medical students from governmental universities in Jeddah was used. A total of 384 students were included. An online questionnaire was provided to eligible students via email and WhatsApp groups, with a secure weblink. The first section obtained demographic and academic level information. The second section included the Oldenburg Burnout Inventory – Student Version (OLBI-SS) and perceived mental health access barriers. The OLBI-SS has 16 items with a four-point Likert scale (1 = absolutely disagree; 4 = completely agree). A cutoff score = 35 indicates high burnout risk (Kilic et al., 2021; Oláh et al., 2022). Ethical approval was obtained from the institutional research ethics committee at King Abdulaziz University, Facuty of Medicine, Rabigh, Saudi Arabia. All participants provided electronic informed consent. SPSS Version 26 was used. Chi-square test analyzed associations between categorical variables. Kruskal–Wallis test analyzed nonparametric quantitative variables. Spearman correlation assessed correlations. Significance was set at p < 0.05. Findings Table 1 shows that the mean age of the students was 22.02 ± 2.94 years, 76% were female and 29.7% had a family monthly income greater than 20,000 Saudi riyals. Almost one-third of students were in the sixth academic year (28.6%). Based on the OLBI score level classification, 96.4% of students had a high risk of burnout, while only 3.6% had a low risk. Table 2 shows that the high risk of burnout was significantly higher among students with the highest monthly family income (>20,000 Saudi riyals) and those in the sixth academic year (p < 0.05). On the other hand, a nonsignificant relationship was found between burnout levels and students’ age or gender (p > 0.05). Students’ responses to barriers that prevent them from accessing available mental health services are summarized in Table 3. The highest score indicating the most frequently experienced barrier was for the statement “Lack of time” (4.61 ± 1.38). The lowest score, indicating the least frequently experienced barrier, was for the statement “I would think less of a person who has received mental health treatment” (2.36 ± 1.86). Table 4 shows that students who had a high risk of burnout had a significantly higher mean score on 12 of the 14 barriers examined (p < 0.05). A nonsignificant relationship was found between burnout levels and the mean scores for “lack of time” as a barrier and “cost” as a barrier (p > 0.05). Table 5 shows that a significant negative correlation was found between the OLBI score and students’ age (r = −0.11, p = 0.03). A significant negative correlation was also found between the total barrier score and the student’s age (r = −0.10, p = 0.049) and academic year (r = −0.13, p = 0.01). Originality/value This study assessed how medical students use mental health services and identified barriers to receiving care, including the stigma of seeking help for mental health issues. A very high proportion of students had a high risk of burnout, and lack of time was the most commonly reported barrier. Correlation analyses revealed that the high risk of burnout was significantly higher among students with the highest monthly family income and those in the sixth academic year. In contrast, a significant negative correlation was found between total barrier scores and students’ age and academic year. Universities should play a role in creating an environment that encourages students to seek mental health treatment by lowering stigma. This could be accomplished by improving access to mental healthcare, increasing transparency about what information is published on academic records, refuting prevalent misconceptions about mental healthcare and raising awareness of resources accessible to medical students. Health education initiatives should positively influence students’ perceptions and attitudes toward mental health treatment and contribute to destigmatizing mental health in the medical school learning environment. There should also be improvements to the infrastructure that supports students’ access to mental health treatments when necessary.

title: A virtual reality cognitive behavioural therapy for anxiety in autistic young people: protocol for an acceptability and feasibility study
abstractText: Purpose Autistic young people often experience heightened anxiety, particularly in social situations. While cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is effective for anxiety, traditional approaches can be difficult for autistic individuals to engage with. Virtual reality (VR) provides an immersive and controllable environment that can enhance CBT delivery through graded exposure and emotion regulation training. This paper aims to describe the design of a study assessing the feasibility and acceptability of a 12-session Virtual Reality Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (VR-CBT) intervention for autistic young people with social anxiety. Design/methodology/approach The study follows a pre-post-test design. Young people with indicated autism and social anxiety aged 12–18years will be recruited from community Children and Young People’s Mental Health Service (CYPMHS) in Hertfordshire. Participants will complete 12-week weekly VR-CBT sessions incorporating psychoeducation, skills practice and graded VR exposure. The authors will evaluate feasibility and acceptability as primary outcomes, alongside assessing exploratory outcomes of pre-post-intervention measures. Findings The study aims to recruit 10–25 participants. Findings will inform feasibility, safety and acceptability of VR-CBT and guide a future large-scale trial. Recruitment and data collection will commence in January 2026. Originality/value This pilot study evaluates a structured VR-CBT intervention for autistic young people with social anxiety. It provides groundwork for scalable technology-enhanced therapy within NHS services.

title: Ethics beyond compliance: employee ESG citizenship as ethically oriented discretionary behavior in organizational governance systems
abstractText: Purpose This study introduces Employee ESG Citizenship – a construct capturing discretionary employee behaviors that proactively support environmental sustainability, stakeholder-oriented social responsibility and governance integrity beyond formal role requirements. Drawing on institutional theory, moral identity theory and ethical climate research, this study aims to examine how employees translate ESG governance pressures into everyday discretionary action and test the construct’s nomological validity against innovative work behavior. Design/methodology/approach A multi-study design comprising three analytical phases was used using two independent samples from ESG-intensive industries within Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor. Study 1 (n = 225, automotive sector) used exploratory factor analysis to identify the construct’s dimensional structure. Study 2 (n = 218, chemical and petrochemical sector) used confirmatory factor analysis to validate a second-order hierarchical model. Study 3 used the same sample as Study 2 to test nomological and incremental validity through hierarchical regression analysis. Findings Employee ESG Citizenship comprises three empirically distinct yet coherent dimensions: Environmental, Social and Governance Citizenship. The second-order model demonstrated excellent fit across indices. All dimensions exhibited strong reliability and convergent validity. Employee ESG Citizenship positively predicted innovative work behavior and explained incremental variance beyond traditional organizational citizenship behavior (ΔR2 = 0.041, p = 0.001). Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and the single-country context may constrain generalizability. Future research should use longitudinal designs, multi-source data collection and cross-national samples to establish causality and test boundary conditions across institutional environments. Originality/value This study makes three contributions. First, it introduces and validates Employee ESG Citizenship as a theoretically grounded, multidimensional construct that extends citizenship theory into the sustainability governance domain. Second, it provides a robust measurement instrument suitable for use in ESG-intensive organizational contexts. Third, it offers empirical evidence that ESG-oriented discretionary behavior captures variance in employee outcomes beyond established prosocial constructs, advancing both citizenship theory and business ethics scholarship.

title: From story to sale: how digital storytelling shapes AR consumers' impulse shopping intention
abstractText: Purpose Digital storytelling has emerged as a catalyst and game changer in the transformative marketing ecosystem through integrative efforts with augmented reality. This study addresses this gap by examining how digital storytelling enhances consumer immersion and enjoyment. It also examines the impact of immersion and enjoyment on consumers' impulse shopping intention. Design/methodology/approach 391 responses were collected from active augmented reality users who had experience with brand storytelling in augmented reality. The data were analysed using a combined importance–performance map analysis (cIPMA) in partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). Findings The findings demonstrate that the importance of four dimensions of augmented reality digital storytelling (narrative structure, perceived aesthetics, self-reference, theming and storytelling) significantly influences immersion and enjoyment and leads to consumer impulse shopping intention. Furthermore, necessity logic complements sufficiency logic by demonstrating that perceived aesthetics constitutes a necessary condition for both enjoyment and immersion. Theming and storytelling impose a weak bottleneck constraint solely on immersion. Additionally, enjoyment and immersion are less restrictive in practice for impulsive purchase intention. This suggests that most respondents already meet the minimum requirements. Consequently, these antecedents function more as performance-enhancing factors than as critical bottlenecks requiring immediate managerial intervention. Originality/value This study pioneers research at the intersection of augmented reality marketing and digital storytelling by demonstrating how narrative, aesthetics, self-reference, theming and storytelling elements can shape consumers' impulse buying intentions through specific prioritising actions with particular dimensions. The findings offer actionable insights for marketers by identifying the performance-enhancing factors (IPMA) and practical bottleneck essentials (NCA) of AR storytelling characteristics that can effectively stimulate impulse purchasing, thereby advancing both theoretical understanding and managerial practice in AR-driven consumer experiences.

title: The emotional labour of knowledge production: an analytic autoethnography of qualitative fieldwork under adversity
abstractText: Purpose This paper examines emotional labour in prolonged qualitative fieldwork and its relationship with knowledge production. Drawing on doctoral research with entrepreneurs in South African township communities, it explores what becomes visible when the researcher's emotional experiences are subjected to critical autoethnographic analysis. Design/methodology/approach The paper adopts analytic autoethnography to re-examine contemporaneous reflexive records generated during three years of longitudinal fieldwork. A corpus of field notes, journal entries and analytical memos was analysed iteratively, informed by emotional labour and decolonial methodology scholarship. Temporal dialogue between the researcher who recorded these experiences and the researcher interpreting them now enabled assumptions about positionality, relationships, authority and the researcher role to be critically examined. Findings Five forms of emotional labour were identified: carrying fear while remaining in the field; earning trust and negotiating access; holding participants' difficult stories; caring while negotiating the research role; and practicing emotional restraint. The analysis shows how emotional labour entered methodological judgements concerning safety, access, disclosure, relationships, interpretation and representation. Reflexive interrogation of these experiences also exposed changes in the researcher's understanding of responsibility, authority and entitlement to knowledge. Originality/value The paper extends scholarship on emotional labour in qualitative research by examining its epistemic significance through analytic autoethnography. It shows how contemporaneous reflexive records can reveal the researcher's emotional and relational participation in knowledge production, while bringing this analysis into conversation with decolonial concerns about power, representation and relational accountability.

title: Serious about silly: the organizational practices behind the creativity of the Savannah Bananas
abstractText: Purpose This study examines how organizational creativity is socially constructed within a high-profile sport organization, the Savannah Bananas. Design/methodology/approach Using a qualitative single-case study design, data were generated through ethnographic observation, semi-structured interviews, organizational artifacts and public digital discourse. Analysis focused on the practices and meanings through which employees described and enacted creativity in everyday work. Findings Findings illustrate how a shared sense of permission to fail and a clear, consistently articulated vision were understood as shaping a creative work environment. Creativity was experienced not in linear stages previously theorized, but as a collective, iterative process involving problem identification, information seeking and idea generation embedded in routine organizational practices. Originality/value The study contributes to the literature by examining how constraints in a sport organization were collectively interpreted and reframed as generative rather than limiting. Rather than attributing creativity to individuals or innovation adoptions, this research highlights how sustained organizational creativity is enacted through shared meanings, routines and interaction.

title: Exploring the effects of group art therapy on emotional well-being among individuals with chronic pain: findings from a pilot study
abstractText: Purpose Chronic pain is a major cause of mental and emotional distress. Its relationship with anxiety, depression, cognitive impairment and sleep disturbances is well documented. The purpose of this study is to explore the effects of an art therapy intervention on individuals with chronic pain observing pain intensity, anxiety, depression, well-being, cognition (memory and attention) and sleep quality. Design/methodology/approach This single-arm pilot study aimed to explore the effects of an art therapy intervention on individuals with chronic pain observing pain intensity, anxiety, depression, well-being, cognition (memory and attention) and sleep quality. An eight-session group art therapy intervention based on the Expressive Therapies Continuum (ETC) model was delivered to 13 participants. Variables were assessed at baseline, mid-intervention, post-intervention and 1-month follow-up, using the Visual Analogue Scale, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, Five Well-Being Index, subjective memory and attention complaints questionnaire and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Findings Clinically significant improvement was observed in pain intensity and overall emotional distress (combined anxiety and depression), with a reduction from 18.2 to 14.9 (p = 0.046), a small-to-moderate effect size (η2 = 0.057) and in terms of well-being, with an increase from 38.8 to 50.2 (p-value = 0.059) and a small to moderate effect size (η2 = 0.053). Practical implications The results contribute to the understanding of this field and complement other non-pharmacological treatments for pain management and associated symptoms, warranting further studies with larger sample sizes and control groups to confirm these findings. Originality/value This studýs preliminary indications corroborate the literature, suggesting that an eight-session group art therapy intervention based on the ETC model may contribute to clinical improvements in the emotional dimension for individuals with chronic pain.

title: Library document repository: a framework for preservation and management of internal library documents
abstractText: Purpose Libraries are information and knowledge resource centres, and while serving their users they need to also effectively manage their own internal documents. The purpose of this study is to explore how school, college and university libraries in Karnataka preserve and manage their internal library documents, assess the relationship between document age and maintenance difficulty and to propose a framework for a Library Document Repository (LDR). Design/methodology/approach The study used a quantitative, cross-sectional survey of school, college and university libraries in Karnataka. Following a key informant approach and purposive sampling, a questionnaire was administered to the head librarians of 154 libraries identified through professional contacts and field visits, and 142 responded (response rate 92.21%): 78 university, 53 college and 11 school libraries. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, cross-tabulation and Spearman’s rank-order correlation, and the findings informed the design of a seven-phase framework. Findings Participating libraries reported greater difficulty maintaining older internal-document collections (rs = 0.52, p < 0.001). About 33.80% of participating libraries had no digital archiving system, while 98.59% believed there was a need for a dedicated library document repository (LDR). These facts led to the development of a seven-phase conceptual framework. Research limitations/implications The findings indicate the need for a dedicated LDR to manage libraries’ internal records. As the study used a purposive sample of 142 libraries in Karnataka, with few school libraries and one key informant per library, the findings indicate patterns rather than support statistical generalization; larger, multistate studies and pilot implementation of the framework are recommended. Originality/value This study focuses on the intersection of institutional repository literature and records management theory. An LDR is proposed and is based on records management principles and in accordance with the Open Archival Information System reference model and the Records Continuum Model. A seven-phase model was developed based on survey results. Document creation/Receipt, digitization, Metadata Assignment, Validation and Approval, Active Access Phase, Retention Monitoring and Secure Disposal were designed for the evidentiary, audit-facing internal document libraries produce to document their operations and are unlike repositories designed to disseminate scholarship.

title: Mentor teachers' understanding of their roles in mentoring pre-service teachers in Tanzania
abstractText: Purpose This study investigated mentor teachers' understanding of their roles in mentoring pre-service teachers during teaching practicum in Tanzania. Design/methodology/approach This qualitative study was conducted in the Iringa and Mbeya regions of Tanzania and involved 8 secondary schools hosting pre-service teachers from three universities with the highest enrolments. A total of 30 mentor teachers with at least 2 years of mentoring experience were selected through purposive sampling. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions, which complemented each other, and analysed using thematic analysis to capture convergence, divergence, and complementarity. Findings The results indicated that most mentor teachers clearly understood their roles in supporting pre-service teachers' professional growth and building interpersonal skills. However, a few had a limited and poor understanding of their responsibilities, leaving pre-service teachers with little or no guidance. Originality/value The study provides context-specific evidence on mentor teachers' understanding of their roles, highlighting the need to strengthen standardised understanding to improve the quality of pre-service teacher education in Tanzania.
