title: Anticipatory information behaviour under uncertainty: temporal, experiential and spatial conditions in information environments for mountain hiking
abstractText: Purpose This study examines anticipatory information behaviour prior to a future activity, focusing on how uncertainty is structured before, rather than during, a planned undertaking – a dimension of information behaviour that remains relatively underexamined. Design/methodology/approach Survey data were collected from 183 Swedish-speaking mountain hikers with experience of multi-day hiking. Exploratory analysis examined variation in pre-hike information behaviour, with temporal distance, experiential familiarity and spatial embeddedness developed as analytical dimensions for interpreting observed patterns. Findings Two complementary patterns emerged. First, whether respondents sought information, when they began planning and how broadly they searched varied across experiential, spatial and temporal conditions. Greater experience and trail familiarity were associated with less information seeking, while greater spatial proximity was associated with less seeking and, regionally, shorter planning horizons. Longer planning horizons were associated with broader searches. Second, information content and source preferences remained comparatively stable across these conditions. This decoupling of information effort from information content is a central finding. Originality/value The study extends information behaviour research into the anticipatory phase and distinguishes information effort from information content as analytically separable dimensions. It identifies effort–content decoupling as a theoretically relevant pattern, suggesting that conditions associated with anticipatory uncertainty need not correspondingly structure all dimensions of information behaviour.

title: Work-integrated learning and graduate employability among TVET students in South-East Nigerian universities
abstractText: Purpose This study investigated the influence of work-integrated learning (WIL) on the graduate employability of technical and vocational education and training (TVET) students in South-East Nigerian universities. It focused on the multiple dimensions of WIL quality (workplace supervision quality, industry placement relevance, intern characteristics, workplace supervisor characteristics and academic supervisor support) and the mediating role of career self-efficacy. Design/methodology/approach A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was used. Quantitative data came from 201 TVET students. They were sampled from a population of 420 across five public universities in South-East Nigeria, using a validated questionnaire. Qualitative data came from semi-structured interviews with 18 purposively selected students and coordinators, analysed using thematic analysis. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, correlation, hierarchical regression, mediation and moderation analyses at 0.05 significance. Findings WIL significantly and positively influenced graduate employability. The expanded five-predictor model jointly predicted employability, with placement relevance emerging as the strongest predictor, followed by supervision quality, intern characteristics, workplace supervisor characteristics and academic supervisor support. Career self-efficacy partially mediated the relationship between WIL quality dimensions and employability. Proactive personality moderated the WIL quality? Career self-efficacy pathway. Inadequate placement slots, specialization mismatch and weak mentorship were the most pronounced challenges. Qualitative findings converged with the quantitative results around mentorship quality, curriculum-industry alignment and structural barriers. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional, single-region design and self-reported measures constrain causal and generalizable claims. Practical implications Findings support standardizing supervisor training, expanding specialization-matched placement slots and strengthening institution–industry collaboration. Originality/value The study extends experiential learning theory and social cognitive career theory into an under-researched South-East Nigerian TVET context. It proposed and empirically tested an integrated model linking WIL quality dimensions, career self-efficacy and employability.

title: Internalising externalities through global technologies: an information systems–based extension of RBV and CBV
abstractText: Purpose This paper aims to advance strategic management theory by proposing iRBV – an Information Systems-based extension of the resource-based view (RBV) and capability-based view (CBV). This essay argues that globally available technologies fundamentally change the role of firm resources and capabilities, enabling firms not merely to respond to market conditions but to reshape the rules by which markets operate. Drawing on RBV and CBV, the author proposes iRBV as a framework for understanding how firms can adopt and adapt global technologies – such as artificial intelligence and blockchain – to internalise externalities and create new markets. Design/methodology/approach This paper presents a viewpoint on how firms can proactively reshape their environment by incorporating externalities into their strategies. The author proposes iRBV – an information systems (IS)-based extension of the RBV, CBV and natural RBV – as a theoretical advancement that enables management scholars and practitioners to develop business models capable of addressing market externalities, including climate change, at the firm level. Findings Through two illustrative cases – ChatGPT and the Libra coin – this essay demonstrates how global technologies can enable firms to reshape markets and internalise externalities that lie beyond the scope of traditional RBV and CBV. Climate change mitigation is presented as one significant application of this mechanism. Research limitations/implications iRBV is presented as a theoretical provocation rather than a fully operationalised framework. Its primary limitation is the reliance on illustrative cases rather than systematic empirical evidence. Future research should develop the microfoundations of iRBV – specifically the routines, heuristics and higher-order capabilities that enable firms to adopt and adapt globally available technologies for externality internalisation. Additional boundary conditions require investigation, including the applicability of iRBV beyond digital technologies, the role of power asymmetries and path dependencies in capability activation and the conditions under which profit-maximisation logic aligns with – rather than diverges from – the internalisation of societal externalities. Practical implications iRBV equips managers with a theoretical lens for identifying externalities as strategic opportunities rather than regulatory obligations. Firms with strong IS capabilities – such as those already deploying artificial intelligence (AI) or blockchain – are well positioned to develop business models that internalise externalities while generating profit. iRBV encourages managers to incorporate a global view of their strategic environment into firm strategy, treating the internalisation of externalities not as a cost of doing business but as a potential source of market dominance. Social implications iRBV suggests that addressing societal externalities – including climate change – need not depend solely on top-down regulation or international agreements. By providing firms with a profit-driven mechanism for internalising externalities, iRBV enables a bottom-up approach in which individual firms take the lead in reshaping market rules and addressing global challenges. This shifts the locus of responsibility from governments and international bodies to firms themselves, driven by intrinsic strategic logic rather than external mandate. If widely adopted, iRBV could contribute to a broader transformation in how business and society relate to one another in the face of global challenges. Originality/value This paper advances RBV and CBV into iRBV, a theoretical extension that positions globally available technologies as levers for internalising market externalities through intrinsic, profit-driven firm strategies. Illustrative examples demonstrate how technologies such as blockchain and AI could enable firms to address climate change – including CO2 traceability, cryptocurrency-based climate incentives and environmentally-linked search restrictions – while simultaneously achieving market dominance.

title: Using grey fractional discrete model to forecast the surface water environment in 312 cities
abstractText: Purpose Accurate surface water quality prediction serves as the foundation for water environment planning and management. This paper proposes a novel multiple fractional-order discrete grey multivariate model to address the limitations of traditional water quality prediction methods. Design/methodology/approach The proposed method realizes the adaptive update of sequence weights through fractional accumulation, and incorporates the particle swarm optimization algorithm for model parameter optimization for enhanced prediction performance. Findings Empirical tests conducted on 312 cities under three scenarios consistently demonstrate the superior predictive performance of the proposed model. Comparative analysis with benchmark models verifies that the proposed model achieves the lowest prediction error. Practical implications The proposed model provides a robust methodological framework for the comprehensive prediction of city surface water quality. It offers support for the formulation of water environment governance strategies and ecological management practices. Originality/value The innovation of the model lies in the introduction of dynamic integration for the original sequence, which overcomes the limitation of static parameters in traditional discrete fractional-order multivariate models. The proposed model is applied to the city water environment index research of 312 cities in China, which substantially enhances the prediction accuracy.

title: Socially responsible leadership and employee green behavior in an emerging economy: mediating role of affective commitment
abstractText: Purpose This study aims to examine the association between socially responsible leadership (SRL) and employee green behavior (EGB), with particular emphasis on the mediating role of affective organizational commitment (AOC) among employees in Ghanaian manufacturing firms. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a cross-sectional survey design, drawing data from employees across 15 manufacturing firms operating within five sub-sectors: Steel and Metal Production, Food and Beverage Processing, Textiles and Apparel Manufacturing, Petrochemicals and Plastics and Pharmaceuticals. Structural equation modelling (SEM), supplemented with bootstrapping procedures, was used to test the hypothesized relationships. Findings The results of this study indicate that SRL is positively associated with EGB and AOC. AOC partially mediates the association between SRL and EGB, suggesting that employees’ emotional attachment to their organization represents one pathway through which perceptions of SRL are associated with workplace environmental behavior. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional nature of the research design constrains causal inference, and reliance on self-reported measures may raise concerns regarding common method variance. Future research should consider longitudinal or time-lagged designs and extend the investigation across different regional or industrial contexts to enhance generalizability and causal robustness. Originality/value This study offers a bounded contextual and mechanism-based refinement of responsible leadership research by examining the SRL–EGB association within purposively selected Ghanaian manufacturing firms and by isolating AOC as a specific emotional pathway. Rather than treating organizational commitment as an undifferentiated mechanism, this study focuses on employees’ emotional attachment, identification and involvement with the organization, which is theoretically distinct from continuance commitment based on perceived costs of leaving and normative commitment based on felt obligation. The findings of this study, therefore, extend existing responsible leadership research without claiming a fundamentally new theoretical integration.

title: A comparative review of quality culture models in higher education
abstractText: Purpose This paper aims to compare eight quality culture models on three questions: how they treat institutional context; how they relate to the structural/managerial and cultural/psychological dimensions; and the extent to which they have been operationalized and theoretically grounded. The comparison identifies areas of consensus, divergence and gaps across the models. Design/methodology/approach A structured comparative analysis was conducted following a multi-stage model identification and selection process using Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC and Google Scholar. Eight models were analyzed across three dimensions: seven met all inclusion criteria and the European University Association Model was retained as a justified exception. Findings All eight models engage with the European University Association’s dual conception of structural/managerial and cultural/psychological dimensions but differ in how they treat the relationship between them. Leadership, communication and participation emerge as recurring binding elements. The analysis identifies a gap among the models reviewed: none combines validated measurement with contextual sensitivity and suitability for resource-constrained higher education institutions. Research limitations/implications The analysis is limited to published English-language sources. It points to the need for a context-sensitive diagnostic instrument. Practical implications The comparison gives institutional leaders a basis for selecting a model suited to their needs, capacities and level of quality culture maturity. Originality/value The paper offers a structured comparative synthesis of eight higher education quality culture models against a common analytical framework. It consolidates a fragmented literature and identifies major conceptual and practical gaps across the reviewed models.

title: Impact pathways: flexibility on the factory floor – expanding gig labor research into the manufacturing context
abstractText: Purpose Manufacturers have begun to experiment with gig labor due to persistent workforce shortages. This article develops impact pathways that specify what manufacturers must resolve for gig labor to function as an effective flexibility lever, and where operations and supply chain management (OSCM) research can advance implementation. Design/methodology/approach We conducted 13 semi-structured interviews, 11 with manufacturing executives and two with CEOs of manufacturing-focused gig labor platforms. Transcripts were analyzed with a Gioia-style coding process. Findings We identify four impact pathways shaping whether gig labor can work in manufacturing: (1) designing flexible workflows for gig labor integration; (2) building plant-level legitimacy for hybrid core–gig workforces; (3) enablement of gig labor through platform mediation; and (4) governing the manufacturing gig labor supply chain. The pathways highlight implications for managers, platform designers, and policymakers. Managers should modularize suitable tasks, design quality into processes, and make the benefits of gig labor visible to incumbent workers. Platforms should embed skills-based matching without increasing income instability, and policymakers should assess whether safety, liability, and worker-classification rules fit flexible arrangements. Originality/value Gig labor research, developed mainly in consumer-facing platform settings, rests on a largely unexamined plug-and-play assumption in which tasks arrive pre-bounded, gig workers operate apart from a permanent workforce, workers are interchangeable, and governance is a two-party relationship between platform and worker. This article shows where each premise breaks down in a manufacturing context and offers a future research agenda for OSCM.

title: How you look determines what you see: a qualitative study of the systemic lens on network engagement in Dutch forensic mental health care
abstractText: Purpose Engaging a patient’s social network in forensic mental health care (FMHC) is widely recognised as important for recovery and risk management. Research indicates that professionals face challenges in shaping network engagement. Research on how professionals view and shape network engagement and its implications for collaboration, remains scarce. This qualitative study aims to explore Dutch FMHC professionals’ systemic lens, focusing on how they view and shape network engagement and address emotional undercurrents in treatment. Design/methodology/approach We first interviewed lead clinicians (LC, n = 5), forensic social workers (FSW; n = 5) and patients (n = 5) at two high-security Dutch Forensic Psychiatric Centres (FPCs). We then conducted two focus groups (n = 8) to discuss the interview findings. Findings Three interrelated themes reflect professionals’ and patients’ perspectives on network engagement: network engagement within the professional role; shaping practice by gaining insight into professionals’ systemic lens; and navigating emotional undercurrents in communication. FSWs serve as link workers in triadic collaboration among patients, social networks and professionals. While their narrative approach supports trust and relational understanding, the lack of explicit guidelines may obscure blind spots and reduce consistency. This highlights the need for ongoing individual and interdisciplinary reflection to support an organisation-wide systemic approach. Practical implications This study provides concrete reference points for professional reflection and supports dialogue on network engagement. Originality/value While tools and knowledge may support network engagement, professionals’ perspectives shape its outcomes. This study provides insight into these dynamics and encourages reflection on practice.

title: When faith sparks innovation: how Islamic work ethics foster kinship employee engagement, knowledge sharing, and innovative work behavior in SMEs
abstractText: Purpose This research aims to explore the ways in which Islamic Work Ethics (IWE) shape kinship employee engagement (KEE), knowledge sharing (KS) and innovative work behavior (IWB) among small and medium enterprise (SME) employees in Lampung Province. The study also tests whether kinship engagement and KS act as mediators and whether psychological safety (PS) acts as a moderator. Design/methodology/approach Using purposive sampling, data were gathered from 218 employees of creative industry SMEs. Respondents completed structured questionnaires distributed through online and offline channels. Structural equation modeling was applied to examine the direct, mediating and moderating paths. Findings The analysis reveals that IWE raises both KEE and KS. These two variables serve as channels through which IWE positively shapes IWB. PS further amplifies the influence of IWE on kinship engagement and on KS, suggesting that ethical values elicit more favorable employee responses when people feel free to speak up and work together. Research limitations/implications Although this study offers valuable insights, several limitations warrant consideration. The findings’ generalizability is constrained by the culturally and religiously homogeneous sample of creative SMEs in Lampung, limiting their applicability to other Indonesian regions or larger firms with different socio-cultural contexts. The cross-sectional design also prevents definitive causal inference, as reciprocal relationships among variables may exist, while social desirability bias could have led respondents to provide normatively acceptable rather than authentic answers. Practical implications The results indicate that SME managers ought to nurture Islamic ethical values and build psychologically safe workplaces to raise engagement, promote the exchange of knowledge and spark innovative behavior among employees. Social implications Reinforcing ethical behavior and PS in SMEs helps build communities that are more cohesive, cooperative and oriented toward innovation, which in turn supports sustainable social and economic development. Originality/value The study deepens current knowledge of the behavioral routes by which Islamic ethical principles encourage pro-social and innovative conduct in SMEs. By combining ethical values with PS, it proposes a new framework that shows how moral norms and a supportive climate together drive innovation at work.

title: Learning at the boundary: how co-design shapes student identity and practice
abstractText: Purpose Co-design increasingly positions students as active partners in educational innovation. Yet, research has focused primarily on design outcomes, with limited attention to what students learn through participation and how involvement shapes their identities. This paper aims to address that gap by examining the experiences of six undergraduate science students who participated in a co-design project developing multi-user virtual reality simulations for science learning. Design/methodology/approach The study conceptualizes co-design as a boundary practice and examines student contributions and learning as occurring at the boundaries between communities. Using a multiple case study methodology, data was collected through pre- and post-session interviews and voice memo reflections submitted after each of three co-design sessions. Analysis proceeded through two coding cycles followed by within-case and cross-case thematic analysis. Findings Findings reveal that students contributed to co-design in three distinct ways: by translating personal learning preferences into design priorities, drawing on knowledge from communities of practice outside their academic programs and embodying personal values about science through the roles they took within their teams. Through participation, students developed boundary crossing competencies, including confidence in sharing ideas, skills in navigating group conflict and an appreciation for differences in collaboration. Three identity trajectories emerged through the boundary learning mechanisms of identification and reflection: reconciling multiple identities, strengthening existing identities and discovering new ways of being. Originality/value These findings position co-design as a transformative learning context for undergraduate students and contribute to a growing understanding of co-design as a site of identity development, not only design production.

title: When AI grades higher: ethical concerns in algorithmic assessment
abstractText: Purpose This study aims to examine the ethical implications of academic grading through the lens of epistemic justice. It investigates whether generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems introduce epistemic asymmetries that could challenge fairness, academic integrity and the governance of evaluative authority. Design/methodology/approach Eighty-seven undergraduate reports included in the study were evaluated by a faculty instructor and ChatGPT-4 using the same rubric. The analysis combined descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, Bland-Altman analysis and paired-samples t-tests. Divergence between instructor and AI scores may reflect differences in how the evaluation criteria are applied. Findings AI consistently assigned higher scores than the instructor and showed no meaningful correspondence in rankings. A systematic bias may suggest structural divergence in evaluative logic. Criterion-level correlations show that AI scoring follows more internally consistent patterns, whereas human judgements remain more differentiated, suggesting different grading standards. These results raise concerns about epistemic consistency in automated assessment. Practical implications The findings highlight the need for governance frameworks for AI grading. Institutions should define transparent policies, assign clear accountability and ensure structured human oversight to prevent algorithmic systems from controlling evaluative decisions. Originality/value This paper reconceptualises AI-mediated grading as an epistemic and governance issue rather than a technical procedure. It explores how automated systems may influence interpretations of academic merit. Empirical evidence of structural divergence between human and AI evaluative logics could support epistemic asymmetries. Integrating epistemic justice, the study provides a novel foundation for governing assessment systems.

title: Too lean? Exploring the nonlinear environmental implications of Factory Physics
abstractText: Purpose Operations and supply chain managers are continuously pulled between efficiency to reduce costs and buffering for resilience. These endeavors are at the heart of Factory Physics, which theoretically defines the levers managers use to control the physics of an organization. However, organizations are also under pressure to incorporate environmental impacts into their decision-making due to consumer and regulatory pressures. With managerial decisions on inventory turnover and capacity utilization having direct environmental impacts, managers are thus challenged to consider environmental performance alongside economic consequences in an increasingly demanding environment. Taking a Factory Physics lens, this research focuses on the environmental impact of inventory turnover and capacity utilization, while considering potential nonlinearities. Design/methodology/approach A high-dimensional fixed-effects approach is employed with a panel dataset of 4,638 operations and supply chain firms from 2002 to 2026. Findings The results suggest that increasing inventory turnover and capacity utilization improve environmental performance. However, there is a nonlinearity: beyond a certain point, additional inventory turnover no longer improves environmental performance. A similar effect is found for capacity utilization when financial leverage is high. Extending this in a post hoc analysis, the findings suggest that capacity utilization is dominant in reducing environmental harm. Further, increasing inventory turnover only improves environmental performance in later stages of the process. Originality/value This research provides a holistic examination of the environmental implications of Factory Physics, considering the multiple levers managers use to manage Factory Physics and the potential for nonlinear outcomes.
venueName: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: A group decision-making model for selecting maintenance providers under hesitation
abstractText: Purpose This study proposes a group decision-making model for selecting industrial maintenance providers that addresses uncertainty and hesitation using hesitant fuzzy linguistic (HFL) methods. Design/methodology/approach The proposed model integrates the evaluation of requirements and criteria through the HFL–quality function deployment (QFD) method, and the assessment of alternatives using the HFL–technique for order preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS) approach. The model was tested in a real-world case study conducted at a railway logistics company. Three decision-makers (DMs) evaluated four maintenance providers based on ten criteria. A sensitivity analysis was performed to assess the robustness of the proposed model. Findings Mobilization time and productivity were identified as the most critical requirements. Service reliability, the willingness to invest in new equipment, safety training, and efficiency received the highest weights. Alternatives A3 and A1 were the top-ranked maintenance providers. Research limitations/implications This model extends previous approaches by explicitly incorporating HFL Terms, enabling DMs to use linguistic expressions to evaluate requirements, criteria, and alternatives. Practical implications The model supports managers in selecting maintenance providers under hesitation by enabling flexible customization of criteria, accommodating group decision-making, and handling uncertainty and hesitation. Originality/value This is the first decision-making model specifically developed for maintenance provider selection that supports group decision-making under hesitation. Furthermore, this study is the first to assign different weights to DMs within an integrated HFL–QFD and HFL–TOPSIS framework, offering a comprehensive approach to supporting complex evaluation processes.

title: Mismatch between original and promotional price colors does not inhibit purchase intention
abstractText: Purpose The primary objective of this study was to investigate whether incongruence between original and promotional price colors in the context of sales promotion would diminish purchase intention. Additionally, the study sought to examine whether this effect depends on product type and elaboration. Design/methodology/approach Five experiments examined the effects of color incongruence between original and promotional prices. Experiments 1 and 2 used a between-subjects design in which original and promotional prices appeared in different color combinations (red, blue, green or black), creating match versus mismatch conditions. Experiments 3 and 4A extended this approach by restricting colors to red and black and adding product type (utilitarian vs. hedonic) or elaboration level (low vs. high), respectively. Experiment 4 B further simplified the design to a two-level color condition (consistent vs. inconsistent) crossed with elaboration. Purchase intention was the primary dependent variable, with attitude towards the ad and willingness to pay also measured. Findings Experiment 1 showed no interaction between original and promotional price colors. Experiment 2 replicated the results. Experiment 3 showed the null effects regardless of product type. Experiment 4A further verified that the null effects still held regardless of elaboration. Notably, in line with the previous experiments, Experiment 4B showed that inconsistency in colors of promotional and original prices did not reduce purchase intention, regardless of elaboration level, even though persuasion knowledge was successfully activated. Originality/value Taken together, the results across five experiments provide convergent evidence that mismatch between original and promotional price colors may not inhibit purchase intention, regardless of product type and elaboration. The present study contributes to understanding the complexity and intricacy in the effects of price color incongruence on consumer responses.

title: Hill Dickinson Stadium: modern construction through design for manufacture and assembly
abstractText: The construction of Everton Football Club’s new stadium at Bramley-Moore Dock in Liverpool represents one of the most significant applications of modern methods of construction in the UK. Delivered within a constrained heritage dockland environment, the project demonstrates the integration of design for manufacture and assembly (DfMA), digital engineering and industrialised construction to achieve improvements in productivity, safety, sustainability and programme certainty. This paper examines how DfMA was embedded across the structural, architectural and building services design, and how it enabled a fundamentally different approach to construction delivery. Particular focus is placed on the prefabrication of structural components, the adoption of modular mechanical, electrical and plumbing systems, the use of schedule-linked three-dimensional (3D) digital simulation (known as 4D) and the development of innovative precast solutions such as double-stepped terracing units. The paper argues that the Hill Dickinson Stadium project illustrates a transition from traditional construction to a manufacturing-led paradigm, offering a replicable model for future complex infrastructure projects.

title: Hill Dickinson Stadium: a digitally integrated approach to modern construction
abstractText: The construction of Everton Football Club’s new Hill Dickinson Stadium at Bramley-Moore Dock represents a leading example of digitally enabled construction in the UK. This paper examines how an integrated digital ecosystem, combining building information modelling, digital twin principles, automated validation systems and cloud-based collaboration platforms, supported modern methods of construction and transformed project delivery. The paper investigates the use of digital tools across design, manufacture and construction, focusing on outcomes such as productivity improvement, enhanced safety, strengthened quality assurance and the creation of a ‘golden thread’ of information compliant with the Building Safety Act 2022. Key innovations included computational fire-stopping validation, paperless reinforcement detailing through Trimble Connect and four-dimensional construction simulation. Using a practitioner-led case study, the authors draw on direct project involvement and access to project records to explore (a) how digital tools were integrated throughout the project lifecycle, (b) the measurable benefits achieved and (c) lessons for future projects. The findings demonstrate improvements in programme certainty, productivity, information management and collaboration. Most importantly, benefits were driven not by individual technologies but by their integration within a digital ecosystem supported by governance, workforce engagement and supply-chain collaboration. While based on a single project, these lessons provide insights for future projects.

title: Hill Dickinson Stadium for Everton Football Club: civil and water engineering
abstractText: Hill Dickinson Stadium for Everton Football Club has been built on the site of Bramley-Moore Dock in Liverpool. The unique location created a series of unique engineering design challenges. These included refurbishment of the existing dock walls, infilling of the dock to provide the platform for the stadium, reconfiguration of the existing waterways of the dock and modifications to the existing boundary wall. All of these designs were undertaken being mindful of the historic setting and this paper discusses how the new designs were influenced by the heritage of the site. An outline of the stadium architecture is described, explaining its position over both existing wharves and the infilled dock, and the creation of a new fan plaza. Civil engineering design of pavements and drainage is discussed, explaining key challenges and care to deal sympathetically and creatively with existing heritage assets such as rail lines and the dock walls. Outline aspects of the stadium framing are presented. The planning and design activities described in this paper demonstrate how heritage values may be successfully balanced with the civil engineering requirements of a major project. Comprehensive site surveys were found to be a critical foundation to this process.

title: Rainfall-triggered railway earthwork instability: thresholds, hydrologic state and operational warning
abstractText: Purpose Rainfall-triggered failures of railway embankments, cuttings and adjacent slopes are managed through rainfall thresholds, geotechnical assessment, monitoring and operating rules, but these elements are often evaluated separately. This review examines how the railway-earthwork evidence progresses from rainfall exposure through hydrologic state and physical response to operational action. Design/methodology/approach A structured critical evidence review was reconstructed from 596 screened records. Of 274 records advanced to the full-text stage, 105 verified full texts were assessed, 20 were excluded after full-text review, 169 had no verified full text and 85 studies were retained. Primary-objective coding was retained for description, while the principal synthesis used non-exclusive study-level coding of rainfall, hydrologic-state, response, operational and validation variables. Findings The retained corpus was predominantly railway-direct (83/85). Primary objectives were mechanism/stability response (29), threshold/risk prediction (28), mitigation/rehabilitation (15), monitoring/condition assessment (8) and operational warning/decision (5). Across all studies, stability/failure evidence appeared in 76, infiltration/seepage in 50 and deformation/displacement in 43. Thirty studies contained an explicit operational action, but only 9 of those reported validation, 3 reported non-failure controls, 1 reported a false-alarm metric, 1 a missed-event metric and none reported a lead-time metric. Practical implications For railway infrastructure managers, rainfall thresholds are best treated as network-level screening tools unless route-specific calibration and asset-state information support stronger decisions. Operational studies should report verified non-failure exposure, false alarms, missed events and usable lead time before a threshold, model or sensor output is relied upon for inspection, restriction, closure or resumption. Originality/value This railway-earthwork-specific study-level evidence-maturity synthesis quantifies where the published evidence remains strong in physical understanding but weak in validated decision support, and identifies the reporting evidence required to move from hazard prediction to defensible railway action.

title: A novel carbon dioxide-cured cement coating for steel slag aggregates to enhance concrete performance
abstractText: The use of steel slag aggregates in concrete supports waste valorisation and sustainable construction, but their poor volumetric stability causes expansion-induced cracking and concrete deterioration. A novel carbonated cement coating was developed through three cycles of cement packaging and carbonation curing. Carbonated cement-coated slag (CCS) was evaluated against water-cured hydrated cement-coated slag (HCS). Mercury intrusion porosimetry and X-ray diffraction characterised the coating’s pore structure and phases; aggregate properties, concrete strength and long-term stability were evaluated. Carbonation reduced coating porosity from 20% to 16% and converted portlandite to calcite and vaterite, forming a denser, more robust coating. Relative to HCS, CCS reduced water absorption from 3.63% to 2.75%, crushing value from 5.14% to 4.07% and autoclave pulverisation rate from 1.82% to 1.07%. CCS concrete reached 41.3 MPa and 51.5 MPa at 7 days and 28 days, respectively. During elevated-temperature curing, it maintained an intact surface and gained strength to 58.8 MPa at 90 days, whereas concrete containing untreated steel slag lost strength and deteriorated. These results demonstrate that carbonation rapidly creates a dense, robust coating that suppresses steel slag expansion, improves aggregate and concrete performance and supports large-scale steel slag utilisation in durable, sustainable concrete.

title: Influence of initial ambient curing on reaction products and strength development in fly ash–silica fume geopolymers
abstractText: Geopolymers blended with silica fume (SF) offer enhanced performance, but the influence of the curing sequence on their properties remains unexplored. This study examines, for the first time, the impact of ambient curing (AC) prior to heat curing (HC) on the strength and reaction products of geopolymer mortars (GPMs) based on SF and fly ash (FA), highlighting their process–structure–property relationships. The initial AC periods were 0–48 h, while HC was conducted at 60°C for 48 h and 100°C for 24 h. Under optimal curing conditions, GPM30 with 5% SF achieved a compressive strength of 54 MPa after initial AC for 48 h and HC at 100°C for 24 h. This was an increase of 42% over GPM26 (5% SF), which reached only 37 MPa after direct HC for 24 h, highlighting the benefit of initial AC. X-ray diffraction and Rietveld analysis confirmed the presence of additional crystalline phases of albite, aragonite and anorthite minerals, indicating the formation of a stable, dense geopolymer matrix under optimal curing conditions. The retention of moisture, as indicated by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy and attributed to the presence of SF, increased the curing efficiency. The results of this work highlight the correlation between curing, aluminosilicate structure and compressive strength, offering insights into optimising curing conditions for SF-blended FA-based geopolymers.

title: Optimization method for spatial robot arm locking-unit layout based on plant root adaptive growth patterns
abstractText: Purpose To address the optimization problem of spatial robotic arm locking-unit layout, this study proposes a collaborative optimization method based on the adaptive growth patterns of plant roots. The approach aims to enhance the fundamental frequency of the robotic arm system while reducing the number of locking units. Design/methodology/approach Drawing upon the adaptive growth principles of monocotyledonous roots, a collaborative optimization model for the position–stiffness–quantity of locking units was established. By constructing simplified spatial robotic arm models and three-dimensional spring-support models, parallel optimization algorithms were used to simulate and optimize the robotic arm’s distributed locking units. The simulation results were compared and verified with the step-by-step optimization approach. Findings The collaborative optimization method significantly enhances the maximum fundamental frequency of the robotic arm while effectively reducing the number of locking units required. Compared to the step-by-step optimization approach, this method demonstrates clear advantages in both dynamic performance and weight reduction. Research limitations/implications This paper does not compare the computational efficiency and accuracy of the collaborative optimization method with those of general optimization algorithms, thereby limiting evaluation of the method’s performance in other aspects. Originality/value By incorporating the adaptive growth pattern of monocotyledonous plant roots into the layout design of space robotic arm locking units, a multi-parameter collaborative optimization model and method for locking-unit position–stiffness–quantity were established. This approach overcomes the limitations of step-by-step optimization methods, offering new insights into the layout design of locking units in complex multi-joint mechanisms such as space robotic arms.

title: Sustainable lightweight concrete: a review of experimental findings and modelling
abstractText: Lightweight eco-friendly concrete (LEC) has attracted growing interest as a sustainable construction material due to its reduced self-weight, improved thermal performance, and potential use of recycled and waste-derived constituents. This review examines the current development of LEC with emphasis on material types, experimental performance, modelling approaches, sustainability assessment, and future research needs. Previous studies show that the incorporation of sustainable and recycled materials can provide promising mechanical, durability, and microstructural performance when suitable mix design and curing conditions are adopted. The review also highlights the role of empirical, numerical, multiscale, and data-driven models in predicting and interpreting material behaviour. However, current findings remain inconsistent because of large variations in constituent properties, replacement levels, curing regimes, testing methods, and modelling assumptions. In addition, sustainability outcomes are strongly influenced by binder-related impacts, transport, and system boundary choices. Overall, LEC shows strong potential for sustainable construction, but further work is required to develop standardised evaluation methods, reliable predictive frameworks, and more application-oriented design guidance.

title: From words to work: how AI social language boosts productivity and creative self-efficacy
abstractText: Purpose While AI agents enhance productivity, they may also threaten human autonomy and creativity in collaborative tasks. Balancing efficiency with individual capability development is key to advancing human–AI collaboration. Design/methodology/approach Based on Emotions as Social Information theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this research conducted two studies to explore how AI social-oriented language influences perceived collaboration outcomes, specifically perceived work productivity and creative self-efficacy. Study 1 employed a questionnaire survey in general work and life collaboration contexts. Study 2 employed a simulated interaction experiment involving specific tasks. Findings Study 1 demonstrated the positive effects of AI social-oriented language on both perceived work productivity and creative self-efficacy, with perceived AI-supported autonomy mediating these effects. Study 2 further supported these relationships and revealed the boundary conditions of task type. Specifically, for creative tasks, highly social-oriented AI language enhanced both perceived AI-supported autonomy and collaboration outcomes, whereas for routine analytical tasks, these effects were not significant. Originality/value This study not only addresses current concerns regarding collaboration performance but also highlights the human-centered value of AI by emphasizing creative potential. It bridges the gap by linking AI language style to these concrete outcomes. The findings enrich the understanding of AI language design in human–AI collaboration and provide both theoretical and practical implications for optimizing AI interaction strategies to improve collaboration outcomes.

title: Hill Dickinson Stadium for Everton Football Club: wind microclimate engineering
abstractText: Hill Dickinson Stadium represents a landmark development for Everton Football Club, combining heritage preservation, modern stadium engineering and environmental sensitivity. Central to the development was the integration of wind microclimate engineering to address pedestrian comfort and safety, which posed an important subject of interest when introducing over 52 000 fans into a highly constrained site in an exposed coastal setting. This paper presents the wind engineering strategy and the steps followed during the design. These began with an assessment of winds at the site. The article highlights the range of investigative techniques employed, including both physical wind tunnel and digital computational fluid dynamics testing to analyse the interaction of site winds with the stadium form and the resulting wind conditions experienced by people. These wind conditions are described both qualitatively and quantitatively with reference to industry standard ‘Lawson criteria’ wind speeds. A wide range of design mitigation methods were considered and employed to ensure the delivery of comfortable pedestrian conditions and bring about other urban design, biodiversity, heritage and operational benefits. Reference is made in the paper to the importance given by the project team to the sensitivity and suitability of the mitigations and to the collaborative design approach that enabled a fully integrated design solution.

title: Effect of operation condition on thermal analysis of typical energy diaphragm walls in cooling mode
abstractText: To provide an accurate assessment of the energy potential to support decisions regarding implementing energy wall technologies and the effective utilisation of underground space and shallow geothermal energy, the effect of operation conditions on thermal analysis of energy diaphragm walls (EDWs) under the combined influences of wall depth (WD) and ground surface temperature fluctuations (GSTFs) in cooling mode is comprehensively studied. The potential influence of the operation condition is first compared through an EDW model test. Then two 3D heat transfer numerical models are built and verified. The findings from a full-scale model based on the climatic and geological conditions in the Chongqing area indicate that the thermal analysis under different operation conditions needs further consideration of WD and GSTFs, or may lead to an overestimation of the energy efficiency. A maximum value of the difference in the thermal efficiencies ranging from 6.4% to 14.4% is obtained for the WD at 10 m between those with and without GSTFs, for intermittent ratio (IR) values from 0 to 3; a maximum difference of 25.4% in the increase of the average daily heat release rate per unit wall area is also observed for the 10 m wall with IR = 3. The results highlight the consideration of GSTFs in the short-term thermal analysis of shallow-depth EDWs under intermittent operation for the accurate thermal assessment.

title: Three-dimensional random field generation and ABAQUS integration for tunnelling-induced sinkhole risk
abstractText: This paper presents a robust methodology for generating spatially correlated three-dimensional random fields and integrating them into the Abaqus software program. The proposed algorithm is verified for both regular and irregular meshes. To enhance applicability, an alternative approach is also presented that generates random fields on regular mesh and maps them onto irregular mesh using Abaqus’s mesh-to-mesh solution mapping. The study identifies a critical relationship between mesh resolution and the scale of fluctuation (L): for hypoplastic soil with spatially varying friction angles, the mesh size must be less than L/3 to ensure modelling accuracy. This methodology is applied to assess the risk of tunnelling-induced sinkholes by analysing cutterhead–soil interaction. Numerical results demonstrate that spatial variability significantly alters support pressure–displacement responses. While homogeneous soil exhibits maximum displacement near the invert, spatially variable soil leads to maximum displacements in localised weak zones with low friction angles. By defining the onset of instability as the point of maximum curvature on the support pressure–displacement curve, the study establishes fifth- and 95th-percentile envelopes. The maximum curvature for these bounds occurs at normalised support pressures of 0.11 and 0.20, respectively. To minimise the risk of tunnelling-induced sinkholes, the study recommends maintaining the normalised support pressure above 0.20.

title: Hill Dickinson Stadium for Everton Football Club: history and heritage of Bramley-Moore Dock
abstractText: Hill Dickinson Stadium for Everton Football Club, completed in spring 2025, was built on the site of Bramley-Moore Dock (BMD) in Liverpool. This paper recounts the history of the site and how this is intrinsically linked to the development of Liverpool. The opportunity is taken to celebrate great former civil engineers, including Jesse Hartley who designed the original dock. The cycles of growth and decline of the docks and city are recounted and their impacts on changes to maritime-related assets since their original construction and use are assessed. The paper discusses how historic artefacts become heritage and how this happened at BMD, including designations by Historic England (HE) and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). Design details are presented in other papers in this special issue. This paper describes the assessment outcomes of HE and UNESCO to the project and some stakeholder reactions to those assessments. Engineering readers are invited to reflect on potential destinies of distinguished but under-utilised engineering assets. The paper is one of a series on the stadium development and sets the scene for others to describe design details to respect the existing engineering heritage of the site and how the stadium design was informed by the heritage of assets on the site and in the area.

title: Unconventional entrepreneurship as a relational pathway to emancipation: entrepreneurs with Down syndrome
abstractText: Purpose This study explores unconventional entrepreneurship (UEs) as a pathway to professional and social emancipation for individuals with Down Syndrome in the United States. It aims to understand how these entrepreneurs navigate challenges, leverage support networks and develop adaptive strategies to create and sustain their specific ventures. The research addresses the underrepresentation of individuals with intellectual disabilities in entrepreneurship studies. Design/methodology/approach The study is based on 24 dyadic interviews conducted with entrepreneurs with Down Syndrome (EwDS) and their caregivers. The research examines multiple dimensions, including individual capabilities, organizational structuring, processual challenges and contextual factors. Through qualitative analysis, the study identifies patterns, strategies and resources that contribute to venture success and social participation. Findings EwDS demonstrate resilience and creativity in overcoming barriers related to stigma, disability and venture management. Their success is strongly supported by family, professional mentors and community networks. Key findings highlight the importance of tailored education, vocational experience, mentoring and inclusive social environments. Unconventional entrepreneurship provides these individuals with opportunities for autonomy, skills development, self-realization and social visibility. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to a reduced sample of entrepreneurs in the United States, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. Future research could expand to other countries and cultural contexts to explore how local disability policies, social norms and support systems influence unconventional entrepreneurship. Practical implications The research offers guidance for policymakers, educators, vocational rehabilitation professionals and community organizations to design support programs that foster inclusive entrepreneurial ecosystems. Key implications include the need for peer-mentoring, tailored funded education, accessible resources and family involvement to enhance the success and emancipation of EwDS. Social implications This research highlights how entrepreneurial experiences among EwDS may help challenge dominant social representations of disability by emphasizing capabilities, participation and economic contribution rather than limitations alone. The findings suggest that UEs may play an important role in reshaping discussions surrounding inclusion within entrepreneurial ecosystems. Originality/value This research makes an original theoretical contribution by focusing on an underexplored marginalized group of UEs and highlighting the interplay between disability, opportunity and support networks.

title: Bending performance and design of a demountable precast steel–UHPC composite beam
abstractText: Increasing attention has been paid to precast steel–concrete composite structures owing to their eco-friendliness, fast construction and reliable quality. Ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC), with low self-weight and outstanding mechanical performance, greatly optimises the performance of precast steel–concrete composite beams. In this paper, the authors propose a novel demountable precast steel–UHPC composite beam with bolt shear connectors designed for disassembly and systematically study its flexural performance and design methodology. Three full-scale specimens are tested to analyse failure modes, load–deflection responses, interfacial load–slip characteristics and strain distribution, revealing the structural cooperative working mechanism. A refined finite-element model is built and calibrated against test results to clarify the internal load transfer mechanism, and parametric analyses are conducted to quantify how key design variables affect flexural behaviour. Theoretical formulas for flexural capacity are derived and verified by way of experimental and numerical data. Combining the generalised strain energy density and the Mann–Kendall criterion, a method is put forward to identify the flexural characteristic values for deeper mechanical interpretation. This research offers solid theoretical and technical references for the engineering design and application of precast steel–UHPC composite structures.

title: Influence of geogrid aperture shape on mechanical stabilization: a coupled FDM–DEM study
abstractText: Geogrids provide mechanical stabilization of granular soils. The efficiency of soil-geogrid interactions depends on many factors, including geogrid dimensions, the relative stiffness of the soil matrix and the geogrid, and the geogrid aperture shapes, sizes, and orientations. To date, various aperture shape of geogrids, including biaxial, triangular, and other multi-axial geogrids have been commercialized. In this study, a coupled numerical methodology is used to simulate cyclic plate load testing and compare two multi-axial geogrids and a recently proposed geogrid structure designed using structural optimization. The vertical displacements of the loading pistons in all cases are recorded and compared. An extrapolation function is utilized to predict vertical displacement at higher numbers of loading cycles. Additional parametric analyses are performed by changing the geogrid rib stiffness, thickness, loading piston diameter, as well as aggregate particle size, and aspect ratio. For the baseline simulation for each scenario, the reduction in loading piston displacement at the end of the extrapolated loading cycles ranges from 14% to 20%, indicating a 6% difference between geogrid configurations. This value changes for the simulated parametric analyses. Based on these findings, the optimized geogrid geometry generally provides superior stabilization of the granular media, as reflected in lower cumulative piston displacements.

title: Bearing mechanism and deformation control of soil–polymer mixed pile groups in sand
abstractText: Driven by the ‘dual carbon dioxide’ strategy and the need for rapid construction, in this study, a novel composite pile group technology is proposed, using quick-setting, high-strength, expansive polymer–sand mixtures. Model tests and numerical simulations were conducted to investigate the effects of pile layout and polymer dosage on composite foundation performance. Results reveal a dual reinforcement mechanism combining ‘cementation’ and ‘compaction’. Pile groups significantly improve bearing capacity and settlement control. At a 10% polymer dosage, the final settlement of a four-pile group is reduced by 34.5% compared to a single pile. Increasing the dosage from 5% to 15% reduces settlement by an additional 31.9%. The pile–soil stress ratio decreases with increasing pile number, indicating uniform load transfer. Pile tip stress decreases with increasing pile number, but increases with higher polymer dosage. Numerical simulations agree well with experiments (errors 5.33–17.45%), confirming that pile groups suppress shallow soil plasticity by way of enhanced pile–soil interaction. This technology offers rapid pile formation, immediate load-bearing capacity and low-carbon-dioxide benefits, supporting resilient infrastructure construction and climate-change mitigation (UN SDG 13), providing a theoretical and experimental basis for efficient foundation treatment.

title: Optimizing energy efficiency capital allocation in public institutional real estate: mixed integer programming versus heuristic approaches
abstractText: Purpose This study examines energy efficiency investments in public institutional real estate, treating building retrofits as capital allocation decisions under budgetary and regulatory constraints. We compare a mixed integer programming (MIP) optimization model with a simplified heuristic approach (HA) to assess whether institutional property owners with limited analytical capacity can achieve near-optimal retrofit decisions without advanced optimization software. Design/methodology/approach The analysis uses operational data from seven buildings on Bogazici University's Kilyos Campus in Turkey, representing a portfolio of residential, academic, administrative and hospitality facilities. Building-level energy consumption, energy costs, carbon emissions and retrofit cost estimates were analyzed using both an MIP optimization framework and a heuristic prioritization model. The models evaluated alternative energy efficiency measures under capital budget constraints and compared portfolio-level investment outcomes. Findings The HA produced solutions within approximately 1–2% of the optimal MIP outcomes under identical constraints, indicating that simpler tools can yield economically efficient retrofit selections for small institutional portfolios. Energy efficiency investments reduce operating costs and carbon emissions while generating additional financial benefits through carbon credit revenues, raising total savings by approximately 19–21% beyond direct energy cost reductions, which can be conservative considering current EU Emission Trading System allowance prices. Practical implications The study offers institutional property owners, universities and public-sector asset managers a transparent, accessible framework for evaluating energy retrofit investments absent specialized optimization expertise. Originality/value The article reframes building energy retrofits as portfolio-level capital allocation decisions, directly comparing optimization-based and heuristic investment selection methods and demonstrates the practical relevance of simplified approaches for small and medium institutional property portfolios.

title: The performance and reusability of chitosan-GAC hybrids for Cd-Pb-Cr contaminated groundwater
abstractText: Heavy metal contamination in soil and groundwater poses severe environmental and health risks, which necessitates efficient, eco-friendly, and sustainable remediation technologies and materials. This study evaluated coconut shell-derived granular activated carbon (GAC) and magnesium oxide (MgO)-modified chitosan hybrids for the removal of Cd(II), Pb(II), and Cr(VI) from aqueous environments, particularly in permeable reactive barriers. Four adsorbents, namely, chitosan beads (Ch-b), GAC-chitosan (GAC-Ch), magnesium oxide-chitosan (MgO-Ch), and GAC-MgO, were synthesised and characterised through Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy. Batch tests showed that MgO-Ch achieved 100% Pb(II) removal in 1 and 7 h for Cd(II), while GAC-Ch removed up to 96% Cr(VI). Equilibrium data fitted the Langmuir (R2 = 0.988–0.997) and Freundlich (R2 = 0.980–0.991) models, with maximum binding capacities of 28–31 mg/g per metal in a ternary system. Dominant mechanisms included chemisorption by way of NH2/OH groups, ion exchange through Mg2+ displacement, and magnesium hydroxide (Mg(OH)2) precipitation. Reusability tests showed chitosan-based adsorbents retained more than 87% efficiency after five cycles, whereas magnesium oxide hybrids demonstrated faster kinetics suited for higher heavy metal concentration scenarios. Magnesium oxide hybrids are ideal for rapid treatments, while chitosan-GAC composites offer sustainable long-term multi-metal removal. These findings support the potential of hybrid adsorbents for eco-friendly remediation of multi-metal-contaminated groundwater and soil.

title: AI framework for construction safety management and standards compliance
abstractText: The construction industry in India's fast-developing Metropolitan Regions experiences high accident rates despite mandatory regulatory frameworks. A large gap exists between standard safety procedures and their on-site implementation due to complex project interfaces and dynamic risks. The objective of this study is to systematically assess localised construction safety conditions and develop an integrated, technology-enabled framework for continuous statutory compliance. Three construction typologies (residential building, road construction, and a water supply project) were audited, revealing critical gaps in safety management. An artificial intelligence-driven framework is proposed to counter these vulnerabilities. Considering a sample of 75 professionals, the study establishes a human-assessed risk baseline using the Relative Importance Index (RII: 0.244–0.781) and Cronbach’s alpha (α = 0.714–0.827). To automate safety enforcement, a pre-trained You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) pipeline detects field hazards, algorithmically mapping them to Indian Standards and Occupational Safety and Health Administration regulations to generate a dynamic Risk Priority Number (RPN: 1–64). A Random Forest Regressor performs predictive risk modelling to identify key site activities influencing high RPN scores. This automated system meets legal standards, aligns with UN SDG 8 to improve social sustainability, and enables objective risk measurement.

title: Analysis of the Merriespruit tailings dam failure using the material point method with NorSand
abstractText: Tailings storage facility (TSF) failures continue to pose severe environmental and societal hazards. Conventional breach assessments often decouple failure initiation from runout, which may limit predictive reliability for certain sites. This study integrates the material point method (MPM) with the critical-state NorSand constitutive model to capture the complete failure sequence, from initial instability through large-deformation flow, using the 1994 Merriespruit tailings dam disaster as a benchmark. The MPM formulation reproduces the observed retrogressive slide pattern and the shape of the final geometry when calibrated against laboratory triaxial data from the in situ tailings for a plausible state parameter value, but underpredicts the runout. The simulated runout appears to be largely affected by the presence of rafts that hinder the flow of liquefied tailings in a two-dimensional simulation, but in three-dimensional reality those tailings would be able to flow around the rafts. Exploratory analyses that artificially remove the rafts result in a good estimate of runout. Comparisons with simulations employing a viscoplastic model based on rheological yield stress provide insight into expectations for low-stress behaviour. It seems promising that a critical-state, large-deformation framework can bridge the present gap between geotechnical failure modelling and hydraulic runout tools for TSF assessments.

title: Deformation and risk assessment of shield tunnelling beneath railway tracks
abstractText: This study investigates the uncertainty in deformation prediction caused by the spatial variability of soil cohesion during shield tunnelling beneath existing railway tracks, using the Ningbo Zhuangqiao railway station undercrossing project as a case study. A cohesion random-field model combined with Monte Carlo simulation was established to evaluate the effects of correlation distance and coefficient of variation (CoV) on ground surface settlement and subgrade settlement. The results show that increasing the correlation distance from 3 m to 12 m enlarges the dispersion of surface settlement and promotes asymmetric settlement profiles, while the railway subgrade remains relatively symmetric due to its higher stiffness. As the CoV increases from 0.3 to 0.5, the standard deviation of ground surface settlement and subgrade settlement increases by 79.68% and 38.89%, respectively, and the exceedance probability also rises. The results indicate that spatial variability of soil cohesion significantly affects settlement dispersion and deformation risk. This study provides a probabilistic reference for settlement assessment and risk control in shield tunnelling beneath existing railways.

title: “An inner journey”: how mentoring others helped international graduate students reimagine themselves
abstractText: Purpose This instrumental case study examined how serving as peer mentors in a six-week peer mentor circle (PMC) shaped international graduate students’ relational learning, reflection and identity development. Design/methodology/approach Guided by Ragins and Kram’s relational mentoring theory and Schlossberg’s transition theory, data were triangulated from observations, focus groups and interviews within one PMC at a large US public university. Findings Findings demonstrated how mentoring operated as a reciprocal, relationship-centered process rather than as a hierarchical exchange. Mentors described (1) mutual learning and connection through storytelling and shared vulnerability, (2) reflective reappraisal of earlier transition experiences that produced closure and self-efficacy and (3) strengthened belonging, communication confidence and professional direction. Originality/value The study extends mentoring research by centering mentor development and positioning PMCs as relational–developmental infrastructures for international graduate student growth.

title: Establishing a seven-factor model of consumer psychological responses to AI advertising
abstractText: Purpose This paper aims to examine the dimensional structure of the consumer psychological response process in artificial intelligence (AI) advertising through the validation of a measurement model consisting of seven constructs to adequately represent the complexity of the “consumer response” process to AI-enabled ads. Design/methodology/approach This research used a survey methodology, with young adults (age group 18–26) from Karnataka, India, as the target respondents. Data were obtained from 324 respondents through convenience sampling in a period of six months (September 2024 to February 2025). Scales that were already validated and adapted were used to measure the constructs, while confirmatory factor analysis was conducted using AMOS and R (lavaan package). For reliability testing, Cronbach’s α and composite reliability (CR) were used; average variance extracted (AVE) was used to assess convergent validity; and the heterotrait–monotrait (HTMT) ratio was used to assess discriminant validity. Findings The results show strong internal consistency, with Cronbach’s alpha ranging from 0.786 to 0.947 and CR from 0.863 to 0.954. Convergent validity is indicated by AVE values ranging from 0.613 to 0.827. Regarding discriminant validity, the HTMT values range from 0.183 to 0.492. The model-fit indices show overall fitness (CMIN/DF = 2.335; RMSEA = 0.064; SRMR = 0.047; CFI = 0.908). These results confirm the proposed seven-factor structure of consumer responses to AI advertising. Originality/value To the best of authors’ knowledge, this study is among the first efforts to validate a multidimensional model that illustrates consumers’ psychological reactions to AI-based advertisements in the Indian market. This study contributes significantly to the literature on advertising and consumer psychology by drawing on both existing scales and novel constructs.

title: Perceptions of health and barriers to using mobile technology for health purposes among adults aged 50 and older in rural China: a qualitative study
abstractText: Purpose Mobile technology has the potential to improve health outcomes, yet smartphone ownership does not necessarily translate into health-related use. This study aims to explore health perceptions, views on using mobile technology for health purposes and barriers to its use among adults aged 50 and older in rural China. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative method was used. Twenty semi-structured interviews were conducted with rural residents aged 50–89 from four villages in Shandong, China. They shared their perceptions of health, sources of health information and their current usage of mobile technology for health purposes. Findings All interviewees had smart mobile phones. They seldom used the phone for health purposes. The barriers of mobile health technology adoption included low literacy, not knowing how to search for health information with mobile phones, fear of losing money through digital platforms, lack of community support in learning and mistrust of local health educators. Research limitations/implications The generalizability of these results may be limited due to the small sample size, the non-probability sampling method and the single location study design. Practical implications To overcome the literacy barrier among the rural late middle-aged and older persons, health apps need to be presented in a visual or audio-based format. National health educators can produce short videos embedded with health messages to engage rural late middle-aged and older persons and build trust before introducing mobile health applications. Promoting adoption of health mobile technology among rural older adults should engage credible official sources and communicate through their younger family members. Originality/value This study identifies barriers to the adoption of mobile health technology. Its findings provide insight for healthcare providers and mobile health technology developers on how solutions can be integrated to improve health outcomes among underserved communities.

title: Beneath the glass ceiling: an examination of gender disparities in Canadian medical education leadership
abstractText: PURPOSE: This study aims to assess gender representation in leadership and academic ranks within Canadian universities and affiliated medical schools during 2020-2021, and describe scholarly productivity by inferred gender. DESIGN/METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: This cross-sectional study identified 1,163 faculty leaders across 17 medical schools and parent universities. Public records, NamSor-inferred gender and Scopus bibliometrics were analysed using contingency tables, Cramér's V and exploratory unadjusted odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Productivity comparisons were descriptive. FINDINGS: Gender was associated with leadership category among 1,110 tabulated leaders (χ2(3) = 24.49, p < 0.001; V = 0.149) and academic rank among 823 leaders (χ2(2) = 16.39, p < 0.001; V = 0.141). Women comprised 30.1% of department heads and 36.1% of full professors. Women had lower odds than men of holding department-head versus other listed leadership roles (OR = 0.46, 95% CI 0.33-0.64) and full versus assistant/associate professorships (OR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.40-0.73). Mean bibliometric measures were higher among men. RESEARCH LIMITATIONS/IMPLICATIONS: These historical data cannot establish current representation or causal mechanisms. Gender inference, differing analytic denominators, unmeasured confounding and unaddressed institutional clustering limit interpretation. Updated longitudinal studies, interviews and validated surveys are needed. ORIGINALITY/VALUE: This national analysis examines gender representation in leadership, academic rank and scholarly productivity across Canadian universities and their affiliated medical schools.

title: Beyond Restoration Survival: The Association Between Full-Coverage Restorations in Primary Dentition and the Development of Permanent Successors
abstractText: Full-coverage restorations are widely used to manage extensive caries in primary molars, to preserve masticatory function and to maintain arch space until natural exfoliation. Restoration survival is reported often, yet far less is known about what these treatments mean for the permanent successors developing beneath them. This narrative review examined the clinical performance of stainless steel, zirconia and hybrid resin crowns in the primary dentition and considered whether their use is associated with developmental or eruptive changes in the succedaneous premolars. We compared published work on restorative materials, clinical and radiographic outcomes, physiological root resorption and treatment-related complications. The available evidence links ectopic eruption, altered crown position and enamel defects to primary molars affected by caries and periapical disease, but it does not establish that the restoration itself causes these changes. Prospective studies following children from intervention until eruption of the successor are needed to separate disease-related from treatment-related effects.
